This goes on to start a table in the\n      // same game, and what the last one left changed can no longer be put\n      // back - its restore resolves symbols belonging to the Cheat Engine that\n      // was ended. So nothing is saved or started while the backend holds this\n      // game, whether the stop that left it so was this one or an earlier one.\n      const unclean = dirtyRunRefusal(live.run_holds);\n      if (unclean) {\n        logUiWarning(\"panel.activation_refused_unclean_game\", { app_id: game.appId, table: table.sha256.slice(0, 12) });\n        throw new Error(unclean);\n      }\n      report(\"Saving the selected table\");\n      // Two independent durable mutations, reconciled one at a time. A\n      // rejected Decky reply is not proof the write did not land, and this\n      // sequence has already stopped the previous owned Cheat Engine by the\n      // time it runs: reporting a committed activation as a failure left the\n      // game without its table and the panel describing state it did not have.\n      // The separate association the selection used to make is gone with it -\n      // saving the profile already puts the selected digest in the table\n      // library, so it only added a second boundary that could fail.\n      await commitDesiredState({\n        subject: \"the selected table and its target process\",\n        write: () => saveProfile(game.appId, appDetails?.displayName || game.name, game.isShortcut, table.sha256, process),\n        verify: async () => {\n          const saved = currentProfile(await refreshStatus(), game);\n          return saved?.table_sha256 === table.sha256 && saved?.target_process === process;\n        },\n      });\n      try {\n        report(\"Recording the authorization for this exact table\");\n        await commitDesiredState({\n          subject: \"the authorization to run this table\",\n          write: () => setExecutionConsent(game.appId, table.sha256, true),\n          verify: async () => currentProfile(await refreshStatus(), game)?.execution_consent_sha256 === table.sha256,\n        });\n      } catch (cause) {\n        throw new PriorDurableCommitError(cause, \"The selected table\");\n      }\n      setTargetProcess(process);\n      setInspection(nextInspection);\n      const nextStatus = await refreshStatus();\n      const nextProfile = currentProfile(nextStatus, game);\n      if (!nextProfile || nextProfile.table_sha256 !== table.sha256 || nextProfile.execution_consent_sha256 !== table.sha256) {\n        throw new Error(\"Backend did not confirm the selected exact-SHA table and authorization.\");\n      }\n      live = await refreshCELaunch(game.appId);\n      const currentRuntime = await refreshRuntime(game.appId).catch(() => null);\n      const existingReady = Boolean(\n        !changingIdentity\n        && hadOwnedCE\n applied\", true);\n          await reconcileStartupCompatibility(game.appId, observed);\n          await stopRequested();\n          report(\"Reading the table's live values\", true);\n          await captureLiveSnapshot(game.appId, nextInspection);\n          await stopRequested();\n          toaster.toast({ title: \"CE Decky\", body: hadOwnedCE ? \"Table switched; the game kept running.\" : toaster.toast({ title: \"CE Decky\", body: \"Table loaded. Cheat Engine connected, but the target process still needs an exact PID selection in Advanced.\" });\n        }\n      } else if (existingReady) {\n        // The owned Cheat Engine this reads through is already running, so this\n        // step owns something the user can stop as much as a launch does.\n        report(\"Reading the table's live values\", true);\n        await captureLiveSnapshot(game.appId, nextInspection);\n        await stopRequested();\n      }\n      await stopRequested();\n      autoloadAttemptRef.current = null;\n      clearAutoloadRetry();\n    } catch (cause) {\n      // The activation transaction spans several independently durable backend\n      // mutations (profile, association, consent, launch/session). If a later\n      // step fails, immediately reconcile Home with the backend before Review\n      // can be dismissed; otherwise the next visible panel could keep showing\n      // the pre-activation table/profile until another unrelated refresh.\n      dropLiveSnapshot();\n      await Promise.allSettled([\n        refreshStatus(),\n        refreshCELaunch(game.appId),\n        refreshRuntime(game.appId),\n      ]);\n      throw cause;\n    }\n  };\n\n  interface PreparedReview {\n    table: TableStatus;\n    inspection: TableInspection;\n    /** What the game's own program holds of what this table scans for, where that is knowable. */\n    scanCheck: TableScanCheck | null;\n    /** Which program that answer is about, so the screen can drop it if the reader picks another. */\n    scanCheckedProcess: string | null;\n    observedProcesses: string[];\n    launchExecutable: string | null;\n    /** What this game's own installed folder holds, for a table that names nothing. */\n    installedExecutables: GameExecutableListing | null;\n    initialTargetProcess: string | null;\n  }\n\n  const prepareReview = async (sha256: string): Promise<PreparedReview> => {\n    const nextStatus = await refreshStatus();\n    const table = nextStatus.tables.find((candidate) => candidate.sha256 === sha256 && candidate.available);\n    if (!table) throw new Error(\"The imported exact table SHA is no longer available.\");\n    const nextInspection = await inspectTableSha(sha256, selectedGameRef.current?.appId ?? null);\n    const existing = currentProfile(nextStatus, selectedGameRef.current);\n    // Review is a detached modal, so the running-process observation has to be\n    // taken here: it cannot arrive from Home after the modal is open. A failed\n    // or empty observation only means the manual entry stays the way forward.\n    const game = selectedGameRef.current;\n    const observed = game\n      ? await refreshCELaunch(game.appId)\n        .then((capability) => capability.game)\n        .catch(() => null)\n      : null;\n    const observedProcesses = observed?.windows_executables ?? (game?.isShortcut ? appDetails?.shortcutExe ?? null : null),\n      initialTargetProcess: existing?.target_process ?? null,\n    };\n  };\n\n  /**\n   * The copy of this table that Cheat Engine will open here, ready to review.\n   *\n   * Two things stop a table working, and one press deals with whichever of them\n   * applies. Cheat Engine refuses a signed table by returning false and saying\n   * nothing; a byte pattern this build of the game does not hold takes out every\n   * cheat one script owns the moment it is enabled. The copy is a table of its\n   * own - a new digest, its own inspection, no origin, because no provider\n   * served these bytes - so it is associated and reviewed exactly like an\n   * import, and the consent is given on its own Review rather than on the press\n   * that made it.\n   *\n   * The program is named where the screen that pressed this knows which one it\n   * is about. \"confirmed\" : \"failed\";\n              } catch (cause) {\n                activation.stopState = \"failed\";\n                throw cause;\n              }\n            });\n          }\n          await activation.stopAttempt;\n          return activation.stopState === \"confirmed\" ? null : \"There is nothing to stop; no owned Cheat Engine was stopped.\";\n        }}\n        onCancel={close}\n      />\n    ));\n  };\n\n  const localArtifactMap = useMemo(() => localTableArtifacts(status?.tables ?? []), [status]);\n  const importedArtifactMap = useMemo(() => importedTableArtifacts(status?.tables ?? []), [status]);\n  // Every table this game imported, still present and verified. Advanced still clears the\n          // whole record; from here, clearing every other game's marks to\n          // retry one table would be a much larger thing than it looks.\n          //\n          // The re-read happens whatever any one of these did, so a failure\n          // part way through leaves the panel showing what is actually\n          // recorded rather than the marks it had before the press.\n          try {\n            for (const sha256 of sha256s) await clearFailedMark(sha256);\n            logUi(\"panel.marks_cleared\", { count: sha256s.length });\n          } finally {\n            await refreshBlockedTables().catch(() => undefined);\n          }\n        })}\n        onSelected={async (sha256) => {\n          const review = await runAction(async () => {\n            await ensureProfileAssociation(sha256);\n            return prepareReview(sha256);\n          }, { failureShownByCaller: true });\n          // Avoid stacking Review above Search and then closing the lower modal;\n          // Decky's modal/focus stack is more stable when the handoff is serial.\n          close();\n          showPreparedReview(review);\n        }}\n        onCancel={close}\n      />\n    ));\n  };\n\n  const openImportedTables = () => {\n    const game = selectedGameRef.current;\n    if (!status) return;\n    logUi(\"panel.modal_opened\", {\n      modal: \"imported_tables\", app_id: game?.appId,\n      tables: importedTables.length, stored: storedTables.length,\n    });\n    showContextModal((close) => (\n      <ImportedTablesModal\n        compatibility={manageCompatibility(status.table_compatibility?.entries ?? The generation moved\n          // with the local answer, so a read in flight cannot put it back.\n          forgetStoredTable(sha256);\n          void refreshStatus().catch((cause) => {\n            logUiFailure(\"panel.status_after_delete_failed\", cause, { table: sha256.slice(0, 12) });\n          });\n        }}\n        onPrepareCopy={async (sha256) => {\n          const review = await runAction(async function prepareTableCopyFromManage() {\n            return prepareTableCopyFor(sha256, null);\n          }, { failureShownByCaller: true });\n          close();\n          showPreparedReview(review);\n        }}\n        onSelect={async (sha256) => {\n          // The same contract as the press beside it. Swallowed\n          // here, a table whose file has gone or whose association could not be\n          // written produced exactly the failure Delete was changed to avoid.\n          const review = await runAction(async function useStoredTable() {\n            await ensureProfileAssociation(sha256);\n            return prepareReview(sha256);\n          }, { failureShownByCaller: true });\n          close();\n          showPreparedReview(review);\n        }}\n        onClose={close}\n      />\n    ));\n  };\n\n  const importPickedTable = async (source: string, memberPath?: string | null, password?: string | null): Promise<PreparedReview | null> => {\n    const appId = selectedGameRef.current?.appId ?? null;\n    const table = await importTable(source, memberPath ?? null, password ?? null, appId);\n    // With no game chosen the file still joins this device's library, which is\n    // what the backend has always allowed: the AppID it takes is optional and\n    // it uses one only to name a table in the not-working record. What cannot\n    // happen yet is the rest - a table is associated with a game and authorized\n    // for one, and there is no game to do either for. Awaited, a status read that failed\n      // for a moment reported the whole action as a failed import, for a table\n      // that is on the device - and the reader's next move is to import it\n      // again. Choose a game to use it.` });\n      return null;\n    }\n    await ensureProfileAssociation(table.sha256);\n    return prepareReview(table.sha256);\n  };\n\n  const openLocalTable = () => {\n    if (!status) return;\n    // Decky's native file picker is itself a detached modal, but unlike our own\n    // showContextModal() wrapper we cannot observe its close lifecycle. The record is kept against the\n   * exact bytes so the same file is not found, downloaded and reviewed again,\n   * and the user is asked once whether to stop using it here.\n   *\n   * Nothing durable is written until that question is answered. Marking first\n   * and asking afterwards meant the answer could not undo what had already\n   * happened without a second write, and every way of dismissing the dialog -\n   * the controller's own Back button included - had to be treated as one of the\n   * two answers. One dialog for one table is the whole message.\n    //\n    // The guard is taken when the dialog opens, not when it is decided to open\n    // one. It used to be taken here, several awaits before `showModal`, and\n    // anything that stopped the wait in between - the panel closing, the idle\n    // latch not coming free - left the table marked as asked about with nothing\n    // ever having been asked. Every later Apply then returned at this line, so\n    // a table that had refused every cheat could be applied for as long as the\n    // user cared to press, and the one question that would have retired it was\n    // never put again.\n    if (refusalDialogRef.current === tableSha256) return;\n    let held = false;\n    const dismiss = () => {\n      if (held && refusalDialogRef.current === tableSha256) refusalDialogRef.current = null;\n      held = false;\n    };\n    // Detached, and only once the global latch is free. Two callers reach this\n    // from inside their own `runAction`, which owns that latch until after the\n    // catch that called this returns - so awaiting the dialog here would\n    // deadlock, and opening it there let the user answer before the latch was\n    // released. That answer was rejected as \"another operation is still\n    // running\" with the dialog already closed: nothing happened, and nothing\n    // said so.\n    // Every branch of this says so. The question is the only thing that gets a\n    // table out of the way, and when it does not appear the user is left with a\n    // notification, a table that still applies, and nothing anywhere saying\n    // which of the several ways to not-ask was taken. It cost two rounds on the\n    // device to find that out once; it should cost a log line next time.\n    const table = tableSha256.slice(0, 12);\n    logUi(\"panel.table_refusal_asking\", { table });\n    void (async () => {\n      // Bounded, because a latch that is never released must not swallow the\n      // question. Two callers reach this from inside their own `runAction`,\n      // which owns the latch until after the catch that called this returns, so\n      // asking immediately let the user answer before it was released and the\n      // answer was rejected as \"another operation is still running\" with the\n      // dialog already closed. Waiting for that is right; waiting for it\n      // forever is how the question is lost.\n      if (busyRef.current) {\n        const waited = await Promise.race([\n          whenIdle().then(() => \"idle\" as const),\n          new Promise<\"timeout\">((resolve) => { window.setTimeout(() => resolve(\"timeout\"), REFUSAL_ASK_WAIT_MS); }),\n        ]);\n        if (waited === \"timeout\") logUiWarning(\"panel.table_refusal_wait_timed_out\", { table });\n      }\n      // Asked whether this panel is still on screen or not.\n      //\n      // It used to be dropped when the panel had gone, on the ground that its\n      // handlers act on refs nobody updates any more. That reasoning was about\n      // a wait that outlived the press; it stopped being true when the answer\n      // became a window this panel opens after closing another one, because\n      // closing that one is itself a way for the panel to go. The question then\n      // fell into the gap it had just made: the notification arrived, the\n      // window did not, and the table went on applying.\n      //\n      // The window is Steam's, not this panel's, so it outlives the panel\n      // perfectly well. Nothing in it reads live state either: the answer\n      // re-checks the selected game against the one it was asked about and\n      // refuses if they differ, which is the same check it always made and the\n      // only one that matters here.\n      if (!mountedRef.current) logUiWarning(\"panel.table_refusal_asked_after_panel_closed\", { table });\n      // What this build of the game does not hold, asked here because it is\n      // what decides whether there is a third answer to offer. A table that\n      // failed on a pattern the program does not have is the case the repair\n      // exists for, and this is the other door to it: Review can only ask the\n      // question when this device knows which program the game runs, and a\n      // table that got past Review unchecked meets the offer here instead.\n      //\n      // Best effort in every direction. This is a question put on top of an\n      // Apply that already failed, and a check that could not run leaves the\n      // dialog the two answers it has always had rather than replacing a\n      // failure the user is being shown with one about diagnosis.\n      const scan = await Promise.race([\n        checkTableScans(tableSha256, game.appId, null).catch((cause) => {\n          logUiFailure(\"panel.refusal_scan_check_failed\", cause, { table });\n          return null;\n        }),\n        new Promise<null>((resolve) => { window.setTimeout(() => resolve(null), REFUSAL_SCAN_WAIT_MS); }),\n      ]);\n      if (scan === null) logUiWarning(\"panel.refusal_scan_check_unavailable\", { table });\n      // Another Apply may have got here first while this one was waiting.\n      if (refusalDialogRef.current === tableSha256) {\n        logUi(\"panel.table_refusal_already_open\", { table });\n        return;\n      }\n      refusalDialogRef.current = tableSha256;\n      held = true;\n      // A window that could not be opened must not leave the table looking as\n      // though it had been asked about: the guard comes straight back off.\n      try {\n        openRefusalDialog(scan);\n        logUi(\"panel.table_refusal_asked\", { table });\n      } catch (cause) {\n        dismiss();\n        logUiFailure(\"panel.table_refusal_dialog_failed\", cause, { table });\n      }\n    })();\n\n    function openRefusalDialog(scan: TableScanCheck | null): void {\n      // What the check found, and whether a copy without it is one the backend\n      // has made and proven. A repair is offered for a proof that passed, never\n      // for the fact that something is missing: a third answer that refuses\n      // itself when pressed is the non-information this product exists to\n      // remove.\n      const missingScans = scan?.missing.length ?? 0;\n      const repairable = Boolean(scan && missingScans > 0 && scan.repairable === true);\n      // The count the table's own patterns are read against, which is what this\n      // check was handed: what it found, what it did not, and what it could not\n      // look for.\n      const scanned = scan ? scan.present.length + scan.missing.length + scan.not_checked.length : 0;\n      // The refusal arrives explaining itself as a different build, which is\n      // a guess made before anything was checked. A check that found every\n      // pattern in the game's own program answers that guess, so the answer\n      // replaces it, here and in the mark this dialog can write. Nothing else\n      // in the dialog speaks when nothing is missing, so the guess used to\n      // stand alone, already disproved.\n      const everyPatternFound = scan !== null && scanned > 0 && scan.missing.length === 0 && scan.not_checked.length === 0;\n      const stated = everyPatternFound && reason.includes(DIFFERENT_BUILD_EXPLANATION)\n        ? reason.replace(DIFFERENT_BUILD_EXPLANATION, EVERY_PATTERN_FOUND)\n        : reason;\n      if (stated !== reason) logUi(\"panel.table_refusal_build_explanation_replaced\", { table, patterns: scanned });\n      // What was missing, and what matched in more than one place. The second\n      // matters most exactly here: a table that failed with every pattern\n      // present says nothing at all otherwise, and a hook Cheat Engine put at\n      // any one of several places is the likeliest reason it did nothing.\n      const scanSentence = [missingScanFinding(scan, scanned), ambiguousScanFinding(scan)]\n        .filter((item): item is string => item !== null).join(\" \");\n      // Said where it applies: a pattern is missing and the script's remaining\n      // code still needs what taking it out would remove, so there is nothing\n      // to offer and the reason is not a mystery.\n      // What is true whatever refused it. The proof fails where the rest of the\n      // script still needs the code that would go, and also where the table\n      // could not be read at all, so naming one of those as the cause would be\n      // stating something nobody established.\n      const noRepair = missingScans > 0 && !repairable\n        ? \" CE Decky cannot make a copy without that pattern and prove the rest of the table is still the table you have, so there is none to offer.\"\n        : \"\";\n      const question = repairable\n        ? \" CE Decky can prepare a copy of this table without the code that needs it, and open it for review. Or stop using this table for this game?\"\n        : \" Stop using it for this game?\";\n      // Keeping the table writes nothing at all, which is also what the\n      // controller's Back button does: Steam routes gamepad cancel to\n      // `onCancel`, so that handler is reached both by the button and by a\n      // reflex press to clear the screen, and neither may leave durable state\n      // behind. Everything durable happens on the explicit \"Stop using it\".\n      //\n      // Where there is a repair it takes the primary answer and stopping moves\n      // to the middle, which is the order the reader is owed: the answer that\n      // might give them a working table before the one that retires it. Where\n      // there is none the dialog is the two answers it has always been.\n      const confirm = showModal(\n      <DeckyConfirmModal\n        strTitle=\"This table did not work\"\n        strDescription={`${stated}${scanSentence ? ` ${scanSentence}` : \"\"}${noRepair}${question} These exact bytes are then marked as not working: the copy stays on this device and search still shows it, but nothing can be set to use it again until you clear the mark, and a source may still offer another version. Keeping it changes nothing.`}\n        strOKButtonText={repairable ? \"Try a repaired copy\" : \"Stop using it\"}\n        strMiddleButtonText={repairable ? \"Stop using it\" : undefined}\n        onMiddleButton={repairable ? traceUiAction(\"panel.table_refusal.stop_beside_repair\", () => { stopUsing(); }) : undefined}\n        strCancelButtonText=\"Keep it\"\n        onCancel={traceUiAction(\"panel.table_refusal.keep\", () => { dismiss(); confirm.Close(); })}\n        onOK={repairable\n          ? traceUiAction(\"panel.table_refusal.repair\", () => {\n              // Captured before the dialog closes, the way the answer beside it\n              // does: the operation this starts runs detached, and without the\n              // press it came from the record shows work nobody asked for.\n              const interaction = currentUiAction();\n              dismiss();\n              confirm.Close();\n              // Nothing durable: the copy is new bytes with a new digest, and\n              // the consent for them is given on the Review this opens. The\n              // table that failed is left exactly as it was, because the user\n              // has not said to stop using it.\n              void repairWhenIdle();\n\n              /**\n               * The copy, once the latch it needs is actually free.\n               *\n               * The same reasoning as the answer beside it, and the same defect\n               * if it is left out: this question is put by a wait that is\n               * allowed to give up on that latch, so the press can arrive while\n               * an operation still holds it and `runAction` refuses on the\n               * spot - with the dialog already closed, which is a press that\n               * looked accepted and produced a message about an operation the\n               * user did not start.\n               */\n              async function repairWhenIdle(): Promise<void> {\n                if (busyRef.current) {\n                  await Promise.race([\n                    whenIdle(),\n                    new Promise<void>((resolve) => { window.setTimeout(resolve, REFUSAL_ANSWER_WAIT_MS); }),\n                  ]);\n                }\n                // Re-read rather than trusting the race: the panel unmounting\n                // releases every waiter without the operation having finished.\n                if (busyRef.current) {\n                  const message = `${game.name} is still busy with the last thing you pressed, so no copy was made. Press Apply again to be asked once more.`;\n                  logUiWarning(\"panel.refusal_repair_blocked\", { table });\n                  setError(message);\n                  toaster.toast({ title: \"CE Decky\", body: message });\n                  return;\n                }\n                // This dialog outlives the press that opened it, and everything\n                // below acts on whatever game is selected now: the copy joins\n                // that game's library and is prepared against the program that\n                // game runs. A game switched underneath it would have made a\n                // copy for the wrong one.\n                const selected = selectedGameRef.current;\n                if (!selected || selected.appId !== game.appId || selected.isShortcut !== game.isShortcut) {\n                  const message = `${game.name} is no longer the selected game, so no copy was made. Select it again and press Apply to be asked once more.`;\n                  logUiWarning(\"panel.refusal_repair_wrong_game\", { table });\n                  toaster.toast({ title: \"CE Decky\", body: message });\n                  return;\n                }\n                try {\n                  const review = await runAction(async function prepareTableCopyFromRefusal() {\n                    return prepareTableCopyFor(tableSha256, null);\n                  }, { interaction });\n                  showPreparedReview(review);\n                } catch (cause) {\n                  // `runAction` has already reported it, in a dialog where it\n                  // can. The table is untouched and the question can be put\n                  // again by the next Apply.\n                  logUiFailure(\"panel.refusal_repair_failed\", cause, { table });\n                }\n              }\n            })\n          : traceUiAction(\"panel.table_refusal.stop\", () => { stopUsing(); })}\n      />);\n\n      function stopUsing(): void {\n          const interaction = currentUiAction();\n          dismiss();\n          confirm.Close();\n          void answerWhenIdle();\n\n          /**\n           * The answer, once the latch it needs is actually free.\n           *\n           * The question is put by a wait that is allowed to give up on that\n           * latch, because a latch that never comes free must not swallow it.\n           * That leaves this press arriving while an operation still holds it,\n           * and `runAction` refuses on the spot: the dialog had already closed\n           * itself, so the user's answer was accepted-looking and then dropped\n           * with \"Another CE Decky operation is still running\" over a table\n           * that went on applying. Waiting here is the same reasoning as the\n           * wait that put the question, one step later.\n           *\n           * If it never comes free the answer is still not silently lost. It\n           * says the withdrawal could not be made and that the table is still\n           * in use, which is a thing the user can act on, rather than a toast\n           * about an operation they did not start.\n           */\n          async function answerWhenIdle(): Promise<void> {\n            if (busyRef.current) {\n              await Promise.race([\n                whenIdle(),\n                new Promise<void>((resolve) => { window.setTimeout(resolve, REFUSAL_ANSWER_WAIT_MS); }),\n              ]);\n            }\n            // Re-read rather than trusting the race: the panel unmounting\n            // releases every waiter without the operation having finished, and\n            // another press may have taken the latch in the gap.\n            if (busyRef.current) {\n              const message = `${game.name} is still busy with the last thing you pressed, so this table was not stopped. Try Stop using it again in a moment.`;\n              logUiWarning(\"panel.table_refusal_answer_blocked\", { table });\n              setError(message);\n              toaster.toast({ title: \"CE Decky\", body: message });\n              return;\n            }\n            try {\n              await runAction(async () => {\n                // Whatever this got through, it says so on the way out. Every\n                // step below is a durable write, the panel that asked is very\n                // likely gone by now, and a partial answer changes the\n                // authority exactly as much as a whole one does.\n                try {\n                  await answerStopUsing();\n                } finally {\n                  notifyAuthorityChanged();\n                }\n              }, { interaction });\n            } catch {\n              // `runAction` has already reported it, in a dialog where it can.\n              return;\n            }\n            // The user has just said this table does not work, so the next\n            // thing they are going to do is look for one that does. The panel\n            // they say it from is usually gone by now - the question closes\n            // Configure cheats, which takes the quick access panel with it - so\n            // this is a request the panel takes when it comes back rather than\n            // a control being focused here.\n            //\n            // Only when the answer went through. A failure puts a dialog of its\n            // own over the panel, and moving the ring underneath that is moving\n            // it somewhere the user cannot see it.\n            logUi(\"panel.focus_requested\", { control: \"search\", table });\n            requestPanelFocus(\"search\");\n          }\n\n          async function answerStopUsing(): Promise<void> {\n            // This dialog outlives the press that opened it, and withdrawing an\n            // authorization always acts on whatever game is selected now. A\n            // game switched underneath it would have had the wrong table\n            // revoked, so the answer only counts for the game it was asked\n            // about.\n            const selected = selectedGameRef.current;\n            // A profile is keyed by AppID *and* by whether the entry is a\n            // shortcut, and the backend treats a write that disagrees about the\n            // second one as a different game: it resets the profile, dropping\n            // the table library and every table's archived preferences with it.\n            // Everything below reads the profile through `selected` and writes\n            // it through `game`, so the two identities have to be the same one\n            // before any of that runs.\n            if (!selected || selected.appId !== game.appId || selected.isShortcut !== game.isShortcut) {\n              throw new Error(`${game.name} is no longer the selected game, so nothing was changed. Select it again to stop using this table.`);\n            }\n            // The mark is written here, on the answer, rather than before the\n            // question. A failure to record it is reported and never stops the\n            // authorization from being withdrawn: the user asked to stop using\n            // this table, and that has to happen whatever the bookkeeping does.\n            let marked: boolean | null = false;\n            // What the backend said when it could not record it. The advisory\n            // list is bounded and refuses rather than dropping somebody else's\n            // decision, and the way to make room is a press on a screen the user\n            // can reach: throwing that sentence away left them with a statement\n            // that something failed and nothing they could do about it.\n            let markFailure: string | null = null;\n            try {\n              await blockTable(tableSha256, stated, game.appId);\n              // Recorded from here on, whatever the re-read of the list does:\n              // reporting a write that landed as one that did not is the\n              // protection failing closed while the user is told it failed.\n              marked = true;\n              await refreshBlockedTables();\n            } catch (cause) {\n              logUiFailure(\"panel.refusal_mark_failed\", cause, { table_sha: tableSha256.slice(0, 12) });\n              markFailure = describeError(cause).slice(0, 240);\n              const listed = await refreshBlockedTables();\n              marked = listed.reason ? null : listed.tables.some((entry) => entry.sha256 === tableSha256);\n            }\n            // One exact-SHA command withdraws authorization, disarms automatic\n            // startup and detaches the selection while retaining local bytes.\n            await revokeProfileTable(game.appId, tableSha256);\n            toaster.toast({\n              title: \"CE Decky\",\n              body: [\n                \"No longer using this table.\",\n                marked === null\n                  ? \"The not-working mark could not be confirmed; refresh the list under Advanced.\"\n                  : marked\n                    ? \"It is marked as not working; clear that under Advanced.\"\n                    : markFailure\n                      ? leadWithCause(markFailure, \"CE Decky could not record that it did not work.\")\n                      : \"CE Decky could not record that it did not work, so search may offer it again.\",\n              ].filter(Boolean).join(\" \"),\n            });\n          }\n      }\n    }\n  };\n\n  const openCheatSelection = () => {\n    const game = selectedGameRef.current;\n    const current = currentProfile(statusRef.current, game);\n    if (!game || !current?.table_sha256) return;\n    if (!currentInspection || currentInspection.sha256 !== current.table_sha256) {\n      // Defence in depth: Home must never open the picker against a table other\n      // than the profile's exact current SHA. A table that ran a cheat\n      // and had it come straight back off is not a thing to configure, and the\n      // question about it opens as a window of its own: raised while this one\n      // is still up it is a window behind a window, which on the device is a\n      // toast saying the table did not work and nothing else, with Apply\n      // available again and no way to reach the one answer that helps.\n      const askAboutRefusedTable = (reason: string) => {\n        close();\n        return recordRefusedTable(game, current.table_sha256 as string, reason);\n      };\n      return (\n      <CheatSelectionModal\n        appId={game.appId}\n        inspection={currentInspection}\n        live={runtimeReady}\n        liveUnavailableReason={beyondLiveControlBudget\n          ? `This table has more than ${MAX_LIVE_CONTROLS} switchable cheats, which is more than CE Decky can read back from Cheat Engine in one go.`\n          : null}\n        pinned={current.pinned}\n        startupPreferences={current.startup}\n        rememberedPreferences={current.remembered}\n        configuredValues={current.configured_values ?? []}\n        onTogglePin={(recordId, pinned) => runAction(() => togglePinnedControl(recordId, pinned))}\n        onTableRefused={askAboutRefusedTable}\n        onSaveConfiguredValues={async (values) => {\n          await commitDesiredState({\n            subject: \"this table's configured values\",\n            write: () => setConfiguredValues(game.appId, current.table_sha256 as string, values),\n            verify: async () => configuredValuesMatch(\n              currentProfile(await refreshStatus(), game)?.configured_values, values,\n            ),\n          });\n          // Catching up Home is not part of the commit: a failed refresh used\n          // to be reported as a failed write of state that is already durable.\n          await refreshStatus().catch(() => undefined);\n        }}\n        onValidateStartupPlan={(remembered, values) =>\n          validateEffectiveStartupPlan(game.appId, current.table_sha256 as string, remembered, values)}\n        onSnapshot={recordLiveSnapshot}\n        onSnapshotInvalidated={() => dropLiveSnapshot()}\n        autoloadEnabled={Boolean(current.autoload_enabled)}\n        onCompatibilityConfirmed={async () => {\n          await refreshStatus().catch((cause) => logUiFailure(\"picker.compatibility_refresh_failed\", cause, { app_id: game.appId }));\n        }}\n        onApplied={async (remembered: StartupPreference[], envelope: RuntimeEnvelope | null, leftOn?: readonly TableControl[]) => {\n          // A selection made with nothing running is only ever going to reach\n          // Cheat Engine through auto-load, so switching cheats on there means\n          // asking for them - turning auto-load on is what the user just asked\n          // for, not a separate decision they have to find afterwards. What was\n          // actually wrong was the disclosure: the first time the user heard\n          // about it was the toast after the commit, so the picker now says it\n          // before Apply instead.\n          //\n          // Both directions ask the same question, or they would fight: has the\n          // user switched a cheat on for this table? Only that is a request to\n          // run something, and only that starts Cheat Engine with the game.\n          //\n          // A stored value is not one. It is the setting a cheat uses once it\n          // is switched on - the same rule the runtime already follows, where a\n          // value belonging to a cheat that is off is kept and not written - so\n          // counting it here armed auto-load for a user who had opened the\n          // picker, typed a number and pinned a row without selecting anything.\n          // A record explicitly switched off is not one either, and arming used\n          // to count any record merely mentioned, so a disarm here would have\n          // been undone by the very next Apply.\n          const autoloadHasWork = remembered.some((preference) => preference.active === true);\n          const armAutoload = !envelope && !current.autoload_enabled && autoloadHasWork;\n          // The last cheat going off with nothing running leaves auto-load with\n          // nothing to do, and armed it would still start Cheat Engine on the\n          // next launch of this game for no cheat at all.\n          const disarmAutoload = !envelope && current.autoload_enabled && !autoloadHasWork;\n          await runAction(async () => {\n            const autoloadTarget = armAutoload || disarmAutoload ? armAutoload : null;\n            // Two independent durable mutations, reconciled one at a time. Both\n            // are exact desired state and fully inspectable, so a lost reply is\n            // reconcilable rather than a failure - but only per write: grouped\n            // behind one commit, a refusal of the second was read as proof that\n            // the first had not happened either, and the selection the backend\n            // had already stored was reported as unsaved.\n            await commitDesiredState({\n              subject: \"the cheats you confirmed for this table\",\n              write: () => setRememberedCheats(game.appId, current.table_sha256 as string, remembered),\n              verify: async () => rememberedMatches(\n                currentProfile(await refreshStatus(), game)?.remembered, remembered,\n              ),\n            });\n            if (autoloadTarget !== null) {\n              try {\n                await commitDesiredState({\n                  subject: \"the automatic loading of this table\",\n                  write: () => setAutoload(game.appId, current.table_sha256 as string, autoloadTarget),\n                  verify: async () => currentProfile(await refreshStatus(), game)?.autoload_enabled === autoloadTarget,\n                });\n              } catch (cause) {\n                throw new PriorDurableCommitError(cause, \"The cheat selection for this table\");\n              }\n            }\n            if (envelope) setRuntime(envelope);\n            await refreshStatus().catch(() => undefined);\n          });\n          close();\n          toaster.toast({\n            title: \"CE Decky\",\n            body: envelope\n              ? []);\n          if (alsoOn) toaster.toast({ title: \"CE Decky\", body: alsoOn });\n        }}\n        onCancel={close}\n      />\n      );\n    });\n  };\n\n  /**\n   * Start Cheat Engine for the exact table this game already authorized.\n   *\n   * Table selection, consent and target process are durable, so the second run\n   * of a game must not have to search for and re-review the same table just to\n   * reach the runtime. This reuses the same attach path as Review and auto-load\n   * and never re-authorizes anything.\n   */\n  const startRuntimeForSelectedTable = () => {\n    const game = selectedGameRef.current;\n    const current = currentProfile(statusRef.current, game);\n    if (!game || !current?.table_sha256 || !current.target_process) return;\n    const tableSha = current.table_sha256;\n    const process = current.target_process;\n    if (current.execution_consent_sha256 !== tableSha) {\n      setError(\"This exact table is not authorized yet. Read again, and only\n      // a proven absence stops the launch: a read that fails proves nothing,\n      // and a game that is running the target is the ordinary case.\n      const live = await refreshCELaunch(game.appId).catch(() => null);\n      const unclean = dirtyRunRefusal(live?.run_holds);\n      if (unclean) throw new Error(unclean);\n      const targetNotRunning = live ? absentLiveTarget(live.game, process) : null;\n      if (targetNotRunning) {\n        throw new Error(`${process} is not running in this game. This game is running ${targetNotRunning.join(\", \")}. Set the target under Advanced, then start Cheat Engine.`);\n      }\n      const nextInspection = inspection?.sha256 === tableSha\n        ? inspection\n        : await inspectTableSha(tableSha, game.appId);\n      setInspection(nextInspection);\n      const observed = await ensureAttachedRuntime(game, process);\n      if (observed.connected && observed.status?.attached) {\n        await reconcileStartupCompatibility(game.appId, observed);\n        await captureLiveSnapshot(game.appId, nextInspection);\n        toaster.toast({ title: \"CE Decky\", body: \"Table loaded and Cheat Engine connected.\" });\n        await announceStartupLeftOn(game.appId, tableSha, nextInspection.controls);\n      } else {\n        dropLiveSnapshot();\n        toaster.toast({ title: \"CE Decky\", body: \"Cheat Engine connected, but the target process still needs an exact PID selection in Advanced.\" });\n      }\n      autoloadAttemptRef.current = null;\n      clearAutoloadRetry();\n    }).catch(() => undefined);\n  };\n\n  /**\n   * Toggle one pinned control straight from the panel.\n   *\n   * Pinning exists so the cheats a user actually uses are one press away, so\n   * this must be a real runtime mutation with the same confirmation and\n   * remembered-state persistence the picker's Apply performs - [] : activeCheatsUnder(control, controls, activeById);\n    for (const { control: child } of under) projected.set(child.id, false);\n    // A script remembered on was chosen in an earlier press, so switching off\n    // the last cheat under it does not take it down; the row pressed is the\n    // user's choice when it is switched on and not when it is switched off.\n    const chosen = rememberedScriptChoices(controls, current.remembered);\n    if (active) chosen.add(recordId);\n    else chosen.delete(recordId);\n    const released = unusedActiveScripts(controls, projected, {\n      chosen,\n      switchedOff: active ? new Set<number>() : new Set([recordId, ...under.map(({ control: child }) => child.id)]),\n    });\n    const releasedRows = released.flatMap((scriptId) => {\n      const script = controls.find((candidate) => candidate.id === scriptId);\n      return script ? [{ record_id: scriptId, active: false, value: null, structure: script.structure, label: controlRowLabel(script) }] : [];\n    });\n    // The scripts above carry the table author's own defaults, so every switch\n    // under them that this press did not ask for is written to its off key in\n    // the same call. Otherwise one pinned cheat switches on everything its\n    // script declares, and the panel counts the one it was asked for.\n    // The scripts this press starts: the ones it has to switch on to reach the\n    // cheat, and the row itself when the row is a script somebody switched on\n    // by hand. Leaving the second one out meant switching a script on from the\n    // panel brought every default it declares with it, which is the whole thing\n    // holding them off exists to prevent.\n    const startedHere = active\n      // Only a script brings defaults: a value with flags filed under it starts\n      // nothing, and holding those flags off wrote cheats the user had on.\n      ? [\n          ...ancestors.flatMap((ancestor) => ancestor.id === null ? `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md`:

```md
# Architecture

## System overview

`src/uiActions.ts` traces owned control callbacks without serializing event arguments and captures frontend interaction identity at operation entry. Its context ends when the synchronous handler returns, so unrelated background work cannot inherit it. `src/useUiSurface.ts` observes modal lifetimes; both write only through the existing bounded `supportLog.ts` ring and support-bundle collector. They do not change RPC arguments, execution consent or backend transaction ownership.

```text
Decky QAM frontend (TypeScript/React)
  ├── controller-only managed CE setup/progress/cancel
  ├── library item and AppDetails integration
  ├── compact current-game home plus Search/Review/Cheats/Advanced modals
  └── @decky/api callables
                  │
                  ▼
Decky backend (Python)
  ├── configuration and diagnostics
  ├── manifest-pinned CE download/native extraction plus CE/table import and immutable storage
  ├── profiles, per-game table-library/autoload state, and exact-SHA consent
  ├── private CE runtime materialization
  ├── session descriptor/control/status protocol
  ├── provider catalog/search/acquisition transactions
  └── on-target validation and provider diagnostics
                  │
                  ▼
DECKY_USER_HOME/.cheat-engine-decky
  ├── ce/installers/<artifact-sha>/
  ├── ce/installations/<artifact-sha>/
  ├── ce/runtime/<versioned-aggregate-runtime-sha>/
  ├── tables/sha256/...
  ├── state/profiles/...   (per-game table library, autoload, consent and cheat choices)
  ├── state/provider_sources.json   (the table sources this user switched off)
  ├── state/game_run_holds.json     (per game: a run a stop left unproven clean, or whose Cheat Engine the user stopped)
  └── state/sessions/<appid>/<uuid>/...

Starting Cheat Engine:
plugin-owned `proton runinprefix` launch into the running game's own prefix
  -> private Windows CE runtime in the game's Wine environment
  -> resident CE Lua bridge
  -> bridge loads the exact session table snapshot
  -> data-only descriptor/control/status files
  -> Decky QAM runtime controls
```

## Production boundaries

- `src/managedSetup.ts` owns one frontend setup observer from start receipt through terminal reconciliation. Cancellation interrupts its pending read and passes the exact result back to the same owner; it never creates a second completion consumer. Lost start, poll and cancellation replies are reconciled against backend capability. An active operation retains monitoring with capped backoff; a confirmed terminal result is not reversed by an optional refresh failure. Unmount releases the observer without cancelling the backend installation.
- Setup read deadlines apply only to capability, status and poll calls. Start, cancel and complete retain their actual mutation promises: neither a deadline nor observer closure cancels a Decky callable. Capability discovering another operation transfers observation to that exact ID, including after a terminal result; the old result never overwrites the newer operation. A failed new start cannot adopt the unchanged terminal ID that was already visible before the request.
- An operation missing from capability is reconciled through its exact idempotent completion RPC, never inferred from an installed path, a reinstall flag or prior handoffs. The owner caches the exact successful receipt through cancellation and completion handling. An unconsumed Cancel preempts ordinary reconciliation reads/backoff; a rejected Cancel receipt still requires backend reconciliation. Owner capability reads have no React publication side effects, so an abandoned read cannot restore stale setup state. A confirmed predecessor completion remains confirmed when observation moves to a successor.
- Review Stop state belongs to one activation attempt. Its completion checkpoints await that attempt's pending Stop, and only a confirmed stop rejects that activation. The panel also drains the attempt's Stop before releasing a failed activation; stale Review callbacks cannot stop a newer activation. Advisory status refreshes do not decide whether the stop RPC succeeded.
- `src/` owns Steam/Decky UI integration because SteamClient APIs are available in the frontend environment. It reads Steam identity (AppDetails, install folders, the shortcut store) and writes no Steam state at all.
- `py_modules/ce_decky/ce_launch.py` owns Cheat Engine process lifetime: exact prefix resolution, live game-container observation, corroborated Gamescope-display resolution, deterministic argv/environment planning, launcher process-group ownership, and isolated-prefix Wine cleanup for self-tests. It is the only component that starts Cheat Engine, and it never touches Steam state.
- `main.py` is a thin Decky entrypoint. It puts `py_modules/` and then
  `py_modules/vendor/` on `sys.path`, so the vendored distributions precede this
  plugin's own package. It then probes `xml.etree` and `html.parser`; when the
  Decky Loader PyInstaller runtime omits those pure-Python stdlib modules, it
  adds the verbatim CPython 3.11.7 `xml`, `html`, and `_markupbase` fallback
  under `py_modules/stdlib_fallback/` without shadowing a complete host stdlib.
- `py_modules/vendor/` is the plugin's third-party Python runtime, committed and
  shipped rather than installed. Nothing here authors it: it is the hash-pinned
  `requirements-runtime.lock` rendered by `scripts/update_runtime_vendor.py`,
  and its identity is the tree digest recorded beside that lock, which the
  repository rules check before anything is packaged. It is pure Python by
  construction, because a native artifact in it would be a binary this project
  ships without reviewing. It is committed because the official Decky Store
  builder copies `py_modules/` exactly as the repository holds it and has no
  dependency-install phase, so a tree produced at packaging time would reach
  this project's own archive and never the Store's.
- `py_modules/ce_decky/` owns filesystem state, validation, profiles, session preparation, runtime protocol, and diagnostics.
- `PluginService.get_status()` includes the exact `plugin_dir` Decky supplied beside its existing user/settings/runtime paths. The authenticated target installer uses that self-report only after the loader inventory and installed metadata agree on the same plugin identity and version; it is diagnostic authority, not a path the frontend may mutate.
- `py_modules/ce_decky/poll_counters.py` holds one process-wide monotonic count, with wall and per-thread processor time, for each repeating path a live session runs. Counts are taken at the RPC boundary for the two calls the panel's detector makes, and inside the launch module for the supervisor's scan and the process-table walk, so an internal caller such as the support bundle is not mistaken for the panel. `PluginService.get_poll_counters()` and its `get_poll_counters` RPC read the snapshot and increment nothing, which is why that RPC exists at all: reading through a counted path would make the reading one of the counts. It is the only RPC the frontend deliberately does not call, recorded as such in `tests/test_rpc_contract.py`, and the same snapshot reaches the support bundle inside `diagnostics_snapshot()`.
- `py_modules/ce_decky/managed_ce.py` owns managed Cheat Engine setup: reviewed-artifact and Proton-tool discovery, and the long-running native extraction transaction. The frontend supplies only an explicit reinstall boolean; it never supplies a URL, executable path, installer arguments, Proton identity, or output path.
- `py_modules/ce_decky/plugin_update.py` decides what a release is and holds no network: version ordering, the release payload, the checksum line for one exact archive, and the durable record. `py_modules/ce_decky/update_manager.py` owns the transaction: the request, the download, the digest check and the spawn, plus the schedule that asks whether a check is owed. `py_modules/ce_decky/decky_control.py` is the bounded client for Decky's own loopback control socket and the two loader routes an install uses; `scripts/target_plugin_install.py` drives the same two routes for a development install and imports them from there rather than repeating them.
- `py_modules/ce_decky/update_runner.py` is a process rather than a component. Decky stops and replaces this backend as part of installing a plugin, so the installer cannot be work on this plugin's event loop: it is spawned detached, in its own session, through a system `python3` rather than Decky's frozen loader runtime, and it outlives the plugin that started it. It decides nothing, verifies the archive's digest again off disk before handing it over, and leaves its outcome in a file the next backend folds into the durable record and deletes. Nothing else in this project starts a process that is meant to survive its own unload.
- `dist/index.js` is committed build output consumed by Decky; `src/` remains its source of truth.

## Storage domains

Three path domains are intentionally separate:

1. `DECKY_PLUGIN_SETTINGS_DIR` for configuration.
2. `DECKY_PLUGIN_LOG_DIR` and `DECKY_PLUGIN_LOG` for Decky-managed logs.
3. `DECKY_USER_HOME/.cheat-engine-decky` for Proton-visible CE, tables, profiles, sessions, cache, and staging.

`DECKY_PLUGIN_RUNTIME_DIR` remains available for ordinary Decky runtime data, but Proton-consumed files use the managed user-home root so visibility follows Valve's home-sharing and Wine `Z:` behavior.

Two preferences and one update record follow those domains rather than inventing a fourth. `update_auto_check` and `mascot_visible` live in `settings_dir/preferences.json`, beside the configuration and deliberately not inside it: `config.json` carries identity and is parsed strictly, so a key an older build does not know costs that build the whole file and the registered Cheat Engine with it, which is what a Steam Deck showed when it updated from this version to the published one. The preferences file is the opposite kind of file - an unknown key is ignored, an unreadable one reads as the defaults - because nothing in it authorizes anything. A configuration that still carries those two keys, from a build that stored them there, has them lifted out and rewritten away once at load, under the same mutation lock every other identity write takes. `state/plugin-update.json` holds what the last check found, when GitHub was last asked as opposed to when it last answered, whether an install is in flight and what the last one did - the two moments are separate fields because the pacing reads one and the screen reads the other, and writing a failed check into the field a screen reads stamped an old finding with today's date; an install and its result carry a generated attempt id, so an outcome written by a process that outlived the backend which started it settles only the attempt it belongs to; `state/plugin-update-result.json` is written only by the detached installer and read and deleted only by the backend, which is what keeps two processes from writing one file. A verified archive an install failed on is kept under the Steam user's home as one file with one name, replaced by the next attempt, removed by a success and by the widest deletion scope, because that is where a user can reach it for a manual install and because it is the only thing this plugin writes outside the directories that sweep clears. What it is - the attempt, the version and the SHA-256 it was verified against - is a record of its own rather than part of what the last update did, and those are two lifetimes: an attempt that fails before downloading anything replaces the second and must not erase the first. One file reused by every attempt also means its presence says nothing about whose it is, so it is offered only while re-reading it reproduces the digest recorded beside it, cached against the file's size and modification time so a status read does not re-hash a megabyte every second. Its proof lives in the state directory and the file itself lives in the user's home, so a deletion scope that clears one and keeps the other carries the proof across rather than leaving a large file with nothing to say what it is. It is also retired when this plugin is already running the version it holds: installing it by hand through Decky is the whole point of it, and that route replaces the plugin without this transaction ever running, so nothing else would ever notice that the file had done its job. The name used to carry the version, which made one file into one per release that nothing ever removed. A pending install and the result that settles it carry the same attempt id and operation id, so a backend that loads while an installer is still out there adopts that install rather than reading the device as one with no update in flight - which is what let a reload start a second privileged install beside the first, and let plugin data be deleted underneath one.

Provider identity is declared once in the provider registry in `providers.py`, which owns display name, rank, adapter kind, host allowlist, base URL, how the provider is reached and whether a download from it begins with a wait it serves out itself, per provider; `catalog.py` derives its host policy from that registry, and search jobs carry their provider with them rather than being matched to a separate list by position. A provider is reached either by a search of its own or only as the exact source another provider's page names, and the registry is what says which: the search's jobs, the per-source summary it returns and the query plan the panel shows are all built from that one answer, so a provider cannot be advertised as a source no search will ever query, and a provider declared searchable with no adapter behind it is reported as a failed source instead of being silently left out. Which of those providers this user actually wants used is a separate small durable store, `provider_sources.py` over `state/provider_sources.json`, kept beside the profile and blocklist stores rather than beside the provider diagnostics in `cache/`, because the cache is offered for deletion as a safe repair and a switched-off source coming back on by itself is not one. It records the providers the user switched **off** and never the ones left on, so a provider added by a later version is on for everyone who never expressed an opinion about it; an unreadable record reads as no refusals, exactly as an unreadable blocklist refuses nothing, and the reason reaches Advanced, the diagnostics snapshot and the support bundle instead of being swallowed. `catalog.py` consults it through a callable rather than a set captured at construction, so a choice written while the service is loaded takes effect at the next search, and it is applied at four points: the search jobs it builds, `_linked_source`, which is the route by which one provider's page names an exact page at another, the cached rows it re-serves, and `resolve`, the one funnel from a selected row to a download. One search runs against one answer: `search()` reads the choice once and publishes it in a context variable that `_linked_source` reads, so a switch pressed mid-search cannot change what that search follows while the roster still describes the selection it began with. Which providers another provider's page may name is declared in the registry as `linked_target` rather than inferred from `discovery`, because GitHub is both searched and linked while three of the five sources are searched and named by nobody; a linked read of a provider that does not declare it is refused as a defect. The frontend's own search cache carries a source-selection revision, because it is keyed by game and query alone: changing the choice forgets every stored outcome, and an answer that lands after the change is stamped with the revision it began under so it is not restored as current. The registry, not the selection, is what builds the search roster, which is what keeps a switched-off source in it as `disabled` rather than omitting it: an answer of no results otherwise cannot distinguish a narrowed search from a build without those sources. It is also the one place that says so, so nothing else in the outcome projects the same fact. The background listing crawl re-reads the selection on every page it owes and stops when its own source is switched off, because it outlives the search that started it by minutes and sleeps through provider cooldowns. Telemetry is attributed by the provider that answered rather than by the job that ran: rows and unreadable pages a linked read produced belong to the provider whose identity they carry, counted as a linked read rather than as a search of a provider no search queried. Deleting the provider cache suspends and drains interactive searches as well as the background listing crawl and downloads, so a search the user closed cannot finish afterwards and write back the files the deletion removed. A corrupt `providers.json` is not repaired by use, because every recording path loads it first and every caller ignores that failure so a broken counter cannot fail a search, so the store carries an explicit `reset()` that Advanced offers. Provider state is split between bounded cache/diagnostics under `cache/` and cancellable artifact staging under `tmp/provider-downloads/`; a diagnostic row whose provider is absent from the current registry is returned only as explicitly retired history. Catalog results expose opaque provider artifact IDs; direct URLs remain backend-only and are not persisted in stale cache state. Artifact-specific browser handoff watches a bounded `DECKY_USER_HOME/Downloads` snapshot and copies a stable regular file into managed staging before validation. A challenged provider search has no trustworthy filename or size, so its backend-owned action disables automatic detection and requires an explicit Decky picker result under `DECKY_USER_HOME`; the selected basename then replaces the action placeholder in inspection and provenance metadata.

`artifact_resolutions.py` stores at most 4096 verified `(provider, artifact_id, artifact_sha256) -> table_sha256` resolutions in `state/artifact_resolutions.json`. Acquisition records only a structurally valid direct CT or an archive with exactly one CT candidate, after verifying the advertised artifact SHA. A refused cheat may still establish that identity; damaged content cannot. The cache contains no URL and supplies provenance only. Clearing a failure changes no resolution, and the resolution refuses nothing by itself.

`table_compatibility.py` stores at most 4096 successful `(app_id, table_sha256)` observations in `state/table_compatibility.json`, separate from consent and the negative blocklist. The service holds bounded pending activation generations in memory, observes the exact successful ACK and a later issued query returning active, and persists when `confirm_table_working` finalizes the successful frontend operation or the backend observes complete successful startup leaf readback from the separate single-ID startup proof, independent of the 128-result diagnostic history. Enclosing scripts are excluded when a requested descendant was also enabled. Backend reload discards unfinished proof. Evidence records the observed target basename, optional PE version, optional Steam build ID, the absolute path that fingerprint was read from, success time and invalidation state. The path is what makes a record comparable after the game stops: the PE version is read from the running game's own executable and a non-Steam shortcut has no build ID at all, so without it a shortcut's proven table had nothing comparable the moment it closed. It is knowable only while the evidence is being recorded, is validated as an absolute path like every other stored string here, and is absent from a record written before it existed, which compares exactly as it did. The target basename is required data validated exactly as a profile validates one, because every comparison against the current profile turns on it; a row without a usable one makes the whole store unreadable, which is a bounded reason and an empty claim rather than a failed status call. Steam build identity is read from one unambiguous AppState manifest under the existing Steam-library discovery authority. Any comparable mismatch requires retest; at least one comparable match and no mismatch permits green; no comparable signal remains neutral. Negative evidence commits a failure epoch with the refusal, and only for a cause that says the table did not work, because a payload or source record answers nothing the positive store holds; it commits independently of positive-store invalidation; clearing the refusal cannot restore earlier success. Both new state files are collected within the existing support-bundle budgets; unreadable records supply no identity or success claim.

`activity_log.py` is the shared log-safety formatter and `OperationRegistry` is the outer asynchronous operation observer. Every registered backend operation logs start and terminal state with a short correlation ID and duration; names come from fixed call sites rather than caller input. High-frequency successful reads/polls are debug-only unless slow. `StateTransitionLog` covers the two facts that are polled rather than called: the runtime envelope, whose attach, PID, target, table-load, startup, window/dialog and last-failed-result state is written once per change and never per poll, and table inspection, written once per digest. Both keep fast-moving counters out of the change signature while still reporting them, and a deleted profile forgets its runtime key so the next game at that AppID is recorded again. Catalog/acquisition, managed setup, runtime materialization and CE launch add domain phase events at the point where they can name the failing boundary. Expected domain/input errors are bounded warnings. Unexpected exceptions are bounded errors with sanitized traceback frame identities, never locals or arbitrary request/response data. These observers retain the component's original error/state contract and re-raise when the caller owns the failure. HTTP client request logging is raised to warning so dependency internals cannot duplicate signed URLs into the ordinary plugin log.

`support_bundle.py` is the read-only collector behind **Advanced -> Report a problem**. The service reads every backend snapshot itself and passes them in, so a probe that raises becomes a manifest note rather than the reason a user has nothing to attach; the module owns only file collection and archive shape. It walks Decky's plugin log directory, `state/ce-launch/`, the settings/profile/blocklist/source-selection/provider-diagnostics files, bounded newest session and self-test directories, and the cheat tables the profiles currently select, then writes one deterministic ZIP under `DECKY_USER_HOME` and prunes all but the newest five it wrote. Every read is bounded, refuses symlinks, and truncates rather than refusing: log members keep their tail, state members their head, and a per-member plus whole-bundle byte budget bounds the result. Session `table.ct` snapshots are excluded because the same bytes are collected once by digest. The frontend's bounded ring buffer arrives as an RPC argument and is revalidated entry by entry before it is written.

The panel keeps that ring buffer in `supportLog.ts`: bounded, in memory, never persisted, read only when a bundle is collected. `runAction` records every user-triggered action and its outcome, a React error boundary inside Decky's own records a render crash before rethrowing to it, and modal opens, game hydration, launch and stop record their identities. Field names matching the backend's sensitive-field pattern are recorded as present rather than by value.

The public acquisition state distinguishes `waiting_provider` from byte transfer. Only the remaining bounded countdown is exposed; transient tokens and URLs remain inside the backend task. A provider whose own chain makes the user wait before any byte moves declares `serves_download_wait` in the registry, and a download from it presents that state in a separate owned modal which continues through optional archive selection/password and import. Playground and VGTimes both declare it, for a countdown their own client contract enforces and, at VGTimes, a one-download-at-a-time rule that queues the second acquisition behind the first. The catalog screen reads that flag off the acquisition it just started rather than recognising a provider ID by name, which is how the second provider with exactly that chain came to be added without the modal; an acquisition whose provider this build no longer declares reads as no wait rather than failing the poll of a running download. the ordinary single unencrypted CT path auto-imports, while even one encrypted archive member requires password input. Closing/unmounting the modal cancels any nonterminal acquisition, and closing a failed completion preserves its diagnostic while still retiring retained staging. Each acquisition serializes its blocking completion and cleanup under one mutation lock, so cancellation either wins and removes staging before import starts or observes the terminal imported result after import finishes; it cannot unlink the source beneath `TableStore`.

What each source's adapter owns on top of that registry and the shared transport, one source per entry:

- **FearLess** is indexed rather than queried, and `fearless-index.json` is a resumable bounded map of forum page offsets to topic IDs/titles only. Page zero establishes its multi-page stride through numeric page-number/offset relations and advertised totals, while a one-page index carries only offset zero and a null stride. A later page may omit independent stride evidence and reuse that proven geometry, but its page number and totals must fit and any explicit stride must agree. Search refreshes page zero before deriving other leading offsets, resumes missing listing pages through one background task, atomically checkpoints bounded batches, and fetches topic pages only after local ranking; unload cancels the crawl and drains any in-flight cache write before shared HTTP closes. When Search was last used is what arms that background pass for a day, and it is durable in two places: inside the index cache, where an ordinary write carries it at no cost, and in `fearless-search.json` beside it, which is a few dozen bytes and has no second writer. A search writes the small one as it happens, because it takes no lock and costs nothing, and the index cache carries the same value whenever a crawl next writes it; load takes the newer of the two. The unload prologue and the background scheduler write only the small one as well, and by then there is normally nothing owed: what they exist for is the search whose own write failed on a device that was full for that moment. Both live in the cache directory, so deleting the provider cache removes the arming with the index it is about.
- **Playground** carries no link until a download starts: its records retain only bounded in-memory file/post identity; acquisition exchanges it for a one-use countdown token and temporary CDN URL, then discards both after the shared downloader starts.
- **VGTimes** owns its whole download chain in `vgtimes.py`, which holds parsing and arithmetic and no network of its own: the catalog service makes every request, so the chain is exercised offline from a captured challenge. Its acquisition request is the one place that sequences those requests, and it returns the exact per-acquisition host policy the page declared alongside the link. The transport grew one form-encoded POST for it, sent once and never redirected, because a POST is not safely repeatable and where a redirected one would go is the caller's decision. `aes_cbc.py` is a decrypt-only pure-Python AES-CBC so that reading one provider's challenge needs no native wheel per architecture. The acquisition manager serializes the downloads of any provider whose request declares that it is served one at a time, which is a property of the request rather than a provider name in the manager.
- **GitHub** carries two routes into the same adapter: a search of the repository index, and the exact repository another catalog's page names. Both end in the same reader, which takes a repository's releases first and its tree only when the releases carry no table. Discovery, ranking and route construction live in `github_discovery.py` and hold no network of their own; the catalog service owns every request, and one shared helper turns an exhausted anonymous budget into the provider cooldown the acquisition layer already waits out. `cache/github-repository-index.json` keeps at most 32 normalized answers keyed by exact query: a one-day fresh answer skips only the scarce repository-index request, and an answer no older than seven days may replace that request only when refresh is unavailable. Release and tree reads are never served from it. A committed table carries a git object name on the artifact record, verified in the acquisition worker beside the SHA-256 check and never exposed through the record's public form.
- **The Cheat Script** ranks its declared sitemap locally, retains only a Yandex public-resource key for each selected row, and asks the anonymous public API for exact metadata during search and a transient link during acquisition. Its request strategy consumes the trusted downloader's one redirect without a third-party Referer, validates the Yandex storage-shard hostname grammar, and returns the one exact runtime host to the shared downloader. Neither transient URL is serialized or cached.

Managed CE setup follows the staged long-transaction model rechecked against Decky Wine Cellar `3445b50f`: backend-owned operation state, bounded download, native format validation/extraction, cancellation, validation before promotion, and no in-place replacement of an installed payload. Extraction writes only to the per-operation owned staging tree; cancellation drains its worker before cleanup, promotion is separately drained across its commit point, and every terminal path removes that exact UUID work tree only after both workers are gone. If cancellation arrives after promotion commits, backend and frontend preserve `completed`, register the exact identity and report the truthful outcome. The service holds a mutation reservation across the whole asynchronous setup, beginning before manager start can publish an operation ID and ending only on failure/cancellation or after the completed installation identity is persisted and the operation is consumed. Session preparation, private-runtime materialization, CE import/clear, launch/autoload and other identity-dependent workflow therefore fail closed instead of racing promotion. The frontend automatically reattaches its monitor to the one surviving operation after reload rather than exposing a second resume/start transition. Because Decky can temporarily retain overlapping observers, the service keeps one in-memory exact-operation completion receipt until the next setup starts: a duplicate completion is read-only and marked as already committed, while a poll of the consumed operation reports it as unknown so a superseded frontend monitor cannot repaint terminal setup progress, and every different or stale operation ID still fails closed. Service unload attempts every subsystem close in dependency order and re-raises the first failure only after the remaining bounded owners have drained. No Proton process, prefix, journal, installer argument or installer execution belongs to setup.


## Managed/imported CE and private runtime

The manifest-pinned managed installation or manually imported fallback is read-only source input after registration. CE Decky records the executable path and SHA, then fingerprints the complete source tree when materializing a runtime. The bridge and deterministic early-load bootstrap are added only to the private copy. Runtime directory identity is:

```text
(CE executable SHA-256, complete source-tree SHA-256, bridge SHA-256)
```

The physical directory uses one versioned aggregate SHA-256 of that tuple so Wine's `steam.exe` proxy does not cross its legacy path limit; the manifest retains the tuple. The source `main.lua` is preserved byte-for-byte under a reserved runtime name, while a generated `main.lua` loads the exact bridge before the preserved source and CE's unordered autorun enumeration. Existing immutable runtimes are reused only after full validation. Damage or identity mismatch fails closed; the directory is not repaired in place. CE bytes never enter Git or the plugin package.

## Table storage and session snapshots

Imported tables are stored by exact SHA-256. Imports durably publish catalogue metadata before blob promotion, so an interruption leaves a named unavailable entry rather than unlisted bytes. No metadata-failure rollback removes a pre-existing blob. At initialization, under the service mutation lock, `TableStore.reconcile_orphan_blobs` scans at most 256 shards and 10,000 entries and reads at most 128 MiB of candidate data. It recreates metadata only for exact-SHA validated CT blobs that have no metadata entry, preserving existing records and all blob bytes. Recovered filenames identify the digest; origin and arrival remain unknown. Recovery and refusals are logged in the ordinary backend log collected by the support bundle. Unprocessed entries remain for the next startup; no status read performs reconciliation. A table CE Decky derived itself records the exact table it came from and the one transform applied, and carries no origin at all; it is otherwise an ordinary stored table and is listed as one. Provenance and profile state are separate from immutable bytes.
