A repository is scored on its name with the words the query supplied removed, because every candidate carries them and they are spelled differently enough to decide the order on their own. Repositories that are Cheat Engine itself, a general table dump, or that name multiplayer cheat techniques anywhere in their name, description or topics are dropped rather than offered and refused later. That last filter names only techniques that are unambiguous on their own; a word an ordinary single-player table would also use, such as unlocking everything, is not evidence, and a word that only means something once its object is named, such as bypassing, counts only when what is being bypassed is named with it. A repository is offered only when it carries a release asset or a table committed in its tree, which is a fact about the repository rather than a guess about its name: the index returns repositories whose whole content is a README promising a table. Releases are read first, because that is where tables usually are, and the tree is read only when they carry none, so an ordinary repository costs one request rather than two.

The two GitHub routes differ in what integrity they can offer, and neither is trusted without one. A release asset may advertise a SHA-256, which is checked against the downloaded bytes exactly as any other provider digest is. A file committed in a tree advertises git's own object name instead, which is not a digest of the bytes alone but is exactly defined and reproducible, so it is verified rather than accepted. That name is never presented as a content digest: nothing that identifies a table by SHA-256 keys on it.

VGTimes has the cleanest discovery shape of any source here. The game is its own path segment and tables have their own listing, so `/games/<slug>/files/cheats/tables/` is a table-only answer and no entry has to be opened to find out whether it is a table rather than a trainer, a save or a save editor. The game index comes from the site's declared sitemap, is cached and ranked locally the way Playground's is, and a search reads a bounded number of ranked games and a bounded number of their entries. Each item page publishes a schema.org block carrying the title, the category that confirms the entry is a table, the author, the date and an exact byte count, and the report linked beside it carries the artifact's SHA-256, so the digest is known before the user chooses the row. The exact filename the site will serve is read rather than derived: a row that cannot say what it would fetch is skipped and counted rather than offered under a name invented for it.

Its acquisition is the site's own chain, and nothing about that chain is written down in CE Decky. The page declares this client's address, its group, the file server it will use and the bundle its client is built from; the bundle names the module a files page loads; that module carries both routes, the fields each is sent, the countdown and what its own client does with every refusal code; and the challenge answer states its key derivation, the header it is keyed by, the image fields it wants read and the shape of the object it expects back. A route or a parameter frozen in the adapter would be a snapshot of one day's site, and the day it moved the adapter would send a confident wrong answer instead of reporting that it no longer understands the contract. The countdown the server enforces is waited out and shown as a countdown rather than left looking like a stalled download. Nothing from the site is executed: the challenge script is unpacked by substitution over the dictionary it carries with it and read as text.

The object that chain builds has one slot a browser fills with an automation probe. CE Decky is not a browser, computes none of it, and sends that slot empty, which the site serves; there is no code path that fills it, and the URL builder refuses a non-empty one. This adapter never describes this client as something it is not.

A guest may have one download open at a time on that source, and the site says so in its own words rather than leaving it to be discovered. CE Decky therefore holds a single download in flight per provider where the provider declares that rule, waits rather than treating the resulting refusal as a failure, retries a bounded number of times reusing the token it already holds, and finally reports the sentence the site would have shown. A refusal that asks for the waiting page again is followed; the site's download queue is a flow CE Decky does not implement, and a file the site says it does not have is not asked for twice.

Open Cheat Tables was one of these and is not any more. Every route this needs from it answers with a site-wide challenge rather than a page, measured with this plugin's own network client, and the only routes that do answer carry no titles to build an index from; the adapter also reached it through a search route that site's own `robots.txt` disallows, which this project does not do.

FearLess discovery never depends on its challenged `search.php` route. Its
public table-forum listing exposes a bounded page count plus topic titles and
IDs, so CE Decky refreshes the leading listing pages during a search, resumes a
bounded local title index in the background, and shows indexed/total page
progress in QAM. What that index holds is said where it decides what a
search can find: the row that heads the results on **Search / Download**
carries it under that row's own press, because a table on a listing page this
device has not read yet is absent from the copy rather than from the source,
and searching again once the index has caught up is what finds it. It is read
from the search's own answer, which already reports that source's index state
on the row it reports for it, so the screen spends no call of its own on it
and says nothing where that source was not part of the search. A page never read is told apart from one only due to be read again, because an aged page is still in the copy and still searched, and only the first kind hides a table. The answer is as old as the search, and a reopened Search shows the one it kept: the wait a source asked for is counted down from when it asked, and counts older than a minute say they are that search's rather than the copy as it is now. The index contains no table bytes, attachment URLs, cookies or
session IDs. A topic the forum has sorted to the end of its own listing with a
leading lowercase `z` is scored and shown under the game's own name: the marker
is the forum's ordering rather than part of the title, and carrying it into
scoring put the topic far below the floor a topic has to clear to be fetched at
all, so those games returned nothing from the source that had them. Only the
lowercase marker is one, because a real game on the same listing is titled
`Z Remastered`. A multi-page stride is accepted only when numeric pagination links
explicitly relate page numbers to offsets, every such relation agrees, and the
result is possible under the listing's advertised page and topic totals. Page
zero establishes and changes that geometry. A later page may reuse the proven
stride when phpBB renders its current number as a non-link and therefore exposes
no independent stride; its `Page N of M` identity and totals must still fit the
known geometry, and any explicit stride must agree. A single-page listing
persists with only offset zero and no invented stride; ambiguous page-zero
pagination costs that listing page instead of creating an index with silent
holes. Search reads page zero before calculating the other leading offsets, so
a changed stride takes effect during the search that first observes it. Search
scores local topic titles first and fetches only the bounded
best-matching topic pages needed to discover their current attachments. A first
search may therefore return fewer FearLess results while the index is still
being built; **Search again** uses whatever additional pages are complete.

Direct backend downloads require HTTPS, explicit provider host policy, redirect revalidation, public-address checks, bounded streaming, content validation, narrow retry behavior, and verified TLS. CE Decky accepts the system resolver as the trusted resolver-to-connect platform boundary; it still rejects a URL if any preflight A/AAAA answer is non-public and repeats validation on every redirect. HTTP 403/challenge marks that provider unavailable for the query, never bypassed; HTTP 429 causes persisted cooldown. That holds at every read a provider owns, not only at its first: a challenge answered by one of its pages stops the rest of that provider's reads for the query and reports it as unavailable, because skipped page by page a provider challenging everything that matched returned an empty list, and an empty list read as a successful search of no results. Rows already obtained before the challenge are kept. That covers every read a provider owns, including the listing that decides which of its pages are worth opening and the crawl that builds its index, because the pages either would go on to ask for are the same challenged site. A source reported as unavailable is also recorded against itself once, by whichever of the job or the search observed it, so the screen that exists to say which source is failing is not reading a value nobody wrote down. A search that finds a provider already inside such a cooldown is not a failure of that provider: nothing is contacted, so nothing is recorded, and the deadline that produced the skip survives it rather than being overwritten by it. A source that answers partly and then stops, from a cooldown it reaches with results already in hand or a limit part way through, reports both at once: the rows it obtained are kept and the source is still reported as unavailable, because reading every returned list as success cleared the deadline that had just been set and hid the outage behind a result count of zero. Each source also has a bounded share of the wall clock, and it is one share for the whole search rather than one per attempt: the retry against the install directory spends what is left of the same budget, because two passes each given the full allowance is the same source holding a controller-visible search for twice as long. A source that has not answered within it is unavailable for that search, and the sources that did answer are delivered rather than held behind it. A source that answered partly and then stopped is reported as partial, with the count of what it did return, rather than as one that found nothing. A page one source links at another is read on the owner provider's terms, honouring its cooldown and recording its refusal against it, while the linking source's own row stands either way. Because that row stands, the linking source discards the failure, so the record kept against the owner is the only trace such a read leaves: it counts the error and names it, and stays narrower than a search failure, because no search of that provider happened, an optional read somebody else's page asked for is not evidence that its own search is broken, and a failure that names no deadline must never write one.

A URL already known while a search runs is held to what the transport will structurally accept, HTTPS with no userinfo on the default port at an exact allowed host, before a row promising a direct download is built from it; resolution and public-address policy stay in the transport, because they need the network and can change between search and download. An entry in a provider's own index is held to the same rule before it contributes identity: an index document must be the document that was asked for, and an entry from another origin is not this provider's, whatever its path looks like. A row whose exact size is already known to exceed what any download route will transfer is not offered. Only an exact size decides this; a described or rounded one stays governed by the streaming bound at transfer time. The source is still reported as unavailable for that query, so it stays distinguishable from a game with no tables. The QAM presents only results CE Decky can download itself; a challenged or browser-only source is counted in the visible per-source summary so a provider that quietly stops working stays distinguishable from a game with no tables.

The Cheat Script discovery follows only the Blogger sitemap its `robots.txt` declares. Search, category, tag and feed routes are disallowed and never requested. Post slugs carry game titles, so all sitemap entries are ranked locally and only the bounded best matches cause a post fetch. Posts before the publisher's measured 2024 migration to Yandex Disk are excluded by sitemap date; an older post edited later may still be checked and then dropped if it contains only the unsupported legacy Mega route. A supported post keeps only its stable public-resource key in the in-memory search snapshot. The documented anonymous Yandex public-resource API supplies the exact served filename, byte count and advertised SHA-256 before the row is offered. Its transient download URL is requested only after selection and stays backend-only. The current downloader hop refuses the third-party post Referer and redirects to a per-resource `s<token>.storage.yandex.net` shard: CE Decky sends no Referer for that artifact, accepts only that bounded HTTPS hostname grammar from the trusted downloader response, and converts the one returned hostname into an exact per-acquisition allowlist before the shared downloader starts. Both transient URLs are discarded after use. Invalid descriptive metadata costs only that value or row, while URL, host, size, digest, archive and table validation remain fail closed.

Playground discovery uses its public sitemap to resolve the game, then the game's own `/<slug>/cheat/table` category listing, whose table entries are the only pages fetched: the same section also holds trainers, save files, save editors, cheat mods, codes, fixes and unlockers, and filenames cannot separate them because a table and a save editor both ship as `.zip`. That listing is not table-only either. A game with no Cheat Engine table still has its trainers and saves listed there, so each entry is read through the category it declares in its own container; an entry whose category cannot be read stays listed rather than being dropped. A listing that carried entries and no table is an answer, not a failure, and the game is reported as having no Playground tables; only an unreadable listing degrades to the unfiltered ranking. Acquisition reproduces the site's public anonymous client contract exposed by its own shipped JavaScript: the backend submits the selected file/post identity to `api/file.download`, waits the bounded advertised countdown, exchanges the transient lock token once, and streams the returned protocol-relative CDN link through the shared downloader. It does not crawl robots-disallowed pagination, extract browser cookies, supply credentials, or automate private Steam CEF/CDP. Lock tokens and temporary CDN URLs never leave the backend and are not persisted or logged. Catalog cache entries contain display metadata and canonical source pages, never transient download state or password hints. Playground's page-supplied byte count is display metadata because target evidence shows it may drift from a valid artifact by one byte; advertised SHA-256, when present, remains the artifact integrity authority and the downloader/inspection bounds still apply independently. A stale cache result is labeled and cannot silently reconstruct an expired direct route without refetching the item page.

During the countdown the acquisition remains cancellable and exposes only a decreasing `provider_wait_seconds` value to QAM. A provider that serves out its own wait opens one controller-owned acquisition modal above the catalog so the countdown, transfer, Cancel action, and any archive member/password choice cannot be stranded below a long result list. Playground and VGTimes are those providers, and each is declared as one in the provider registry rather than recognised by name at the screen: both make a guest sit through a countdown their own client contract states, and VGTimes serves a guest one download at a time, so its second acquisition waits for the first as well. A single unencrypted `.CT` imports automatically; a single encrypted member stays in that modal for password input. Import and detached-modal cleanup are serialized so late unmount cancellation cannot remove staging beneath a blocking import, and the acquisition modal closes before Search performs the serial exact-SHA Review handoff. Execution still waits for Review. HTTP 429 preserves bounded `Retry-After` input in provider diagnostics and prevents immediate repeated attempts; the FearLess background index atomically checkpoints its progress, pauses for the same bounded cooldown and resumes the missing listing page instead of spinning or restarting. An acquisition step that answers HTTP 429 is a wait rather than a failure: the acquisition returns to the same cancellable waiting state, shows that the provider is rate limiting rather than preparing anything, and retries a bounded number of times, honouring a bounded `Retry-After` when the provider names one and using a short interactive backoff when it does not. This covers the request that asks a provider for a transient link as well as the artifact transfer itself, because nothing has been spent when that request is refused. The one exception is a limit that lands on Playground's lock exchange, after its one-shot countdown token has been issued and its countdown served: waiting there would replay a handshake the provider has already closed, so that attempt fails with the provider's status. Waiting deliberately does not adopt the background index's own cooldown, whose default minute is longer than the throttle observed on the target, and an attempt fails with the provider's status once the bounded attempts are spent. Nothing else on the download path adopts it either: a table the user has selected is asked for, and a cooldown a failed search recorded never refuses that download before the provider has been given the chance to answer. A wait a provider's own resolver serves out says which kind it is, because a countdown every guest sits through and a provider refusing right now are different things to be told, and a limit a resolver handles inside itself is the only place that refusal is visible. A provider whose own rule is one download at a time keeps its rate limits inside its own resolver, because restarting such a chain would ask for a second handshake rather than repeat a request, and a limit that cannot be waited out there leaves the resolver marked as one the retry layer must not simply run again. A rate limit that was waited out and recovered from is counted in provider diagnostics, with the wait it cost, separately from failed downloads and from the persisted cooldown a terminal 429 sets: a provider that throttles every transfer is otherwise indistinguishable from one that serves files immediately. Every screen that names a provider names the one the artifact is actually coming from.

The frontend selects `provider + artifact_id`; it never supplies a download URL. Direct artifacts pass through the existing archive/table validators and content-addressed store. Table metadata records a bounded, deduplicated origin history per exact SHA. Import remains separate from exact-SHA execution consent.

Provider UI state is bound to exact game identity, including AppID and Steam-vs-shortcut kind. Identity changes invalidate async generations during the committed UI transition, clear old results, and best-effort cancel both already-known and late-returning nonterminal acquisitions before their result can be adopted by the new game context.

## 13. Lifecycle and removal

Frontend routes, subscriptions, patches, listeners, timers, and debounced writes are registered once and removed on dismount. An in-flight read of live cheat state is aborted there too: a refresh walks every actionable record of the table in chunks, which for a large table is over a hundred bridge round-trips, and a dismissed panel must stop that work rather than run it to completion against a component that no longer exists. A mutation the user asked for is not abandoned this way; only reads the panel started for itself. A mutation that outlives its panel therefore completes and reports to a component that is gone, which is an ordinary event rather than an error case: Steam recreates the quick-access browser view while the plugin is working, including when a game returns to the foreground because CE Decky stopped Cheat Engine. Home does not poll its own state, so it re-reads the profile authority and the record of tables that did not work every time the quick-access panel is shown again, and once more as soon as its first status arrives on a panel that was created while the panel was already on screen, which never sees a visibility change at all. That immediate read is issued one round trip after the panel's own first one rather than at a moment related to the write it is racing, so it is followed by a single bounded catch-up read past the far side of the window actually observed on the target. It happens once per panel, behind the first reread that panel performs, and a panel hidden or dismounted before it fires cancels it, because being shown again re-reads anyway. That is what keeps a panel from presenting an execution authorization, a table selection or a mark that was changed while it was being replaced. A loader that cannot report panel visibility loses the re-read, never the panel. Backend cooperative operations are cancelled and awaited on unload. Bounded worker-thread filesystem mutations are drained before unload completes and never promote state after shutdown.

CE Decky can install its own newer release, and does so only on an explicit press. What that press is worth is decided in this order: the newest stable GitHub release is read again at the press rather than taken from the last check, it must be the version the confirmation named, its tag must parse as a version this project publishes and be strictly newer than the running one, the release must carry both its archive and the checksum file published beside it, and the downloaded archive must match the digest that file states. The version is carried from the confirmation into the transaction because the press is consent for a named version: a release published between the screen and the request stops the update and asks again rather than installing something nobody was shown. A prerelease is never offered. An update is installed only where no game is running, because installing replaces this backend and restarts Steam's interface. Checking for one and offering it go on during a game, and both Update presses, on Home and in Advanced, stay where they are: a press asks the backend the question its own start check asks and, where a game is running or that cannot be established, says to close it and opens nothing, leaving Advanced open. A game there is any process Steam launched as one, other than CE Decky's own Cheat Engine: one carrying a non-zero `SteamAppId`, or, for a non-Steam shortcut that carries only that, its 64-bit `SteamGameId`, which is no AppID a profile is keyed by and is still evidence that something is running. Choosing a game asks the stricter question of which AppIDs are running, and that answer is not this one. The backend refuses the same start before reserving or downloading anything, whoever asks, and a process scan that could not finish is not one that found nothing. What CE Decky is doing itself counts as well as what the process table says, so a start on its way or a Cheat Engine it owns holds an update even where no game is observed. Only then is the archive handed to Decky's own loader over its loopback control socket, and not while this backend holds something only in memory: a Cheat Engine stop still deciding what it left, whose transition and the hold it is about to write exist only in the backend the install replaces, or a hold whose write to disk failed, which the next backend would not read. The same no-running-game answer is taken again at that moment, because a game started during the download holds the install too; while that is what the install waits for it asks every few seconds rather than twice a second, since each ask walks the process table on a device somebody is playing on, and every ask is fresh, so the one that finds no game is the one that installs. The verified update waits, still cancellable, says which of these it is waiting for, writes the unsaved holds again as it waits, and gives up with that reason after a minute rather than install over either. A hold already on disk does not hold an update, since the next backend reads it and refuses as this one does, and neither does a record that could not be read, which refuses every start there as well. The decision to install is taken under the same lock a stop begins under, and once it is taken a stop is refused until CE Decky is back, and so is every Cheat Engine start, since one it started would have nothing left to own it, because the backend that loads next recovers the Cheat Engine this one owned and stops it with a transaction of its own. That loader is what installs plugins on this device; nothing here writes into the plugin directory, and nothing needs root. Because that install stops and replaces this backend, the process performing it is detached and outlives the plugin, and the record it leaves is read by the backend that loads next: an update that failed keeps the verified archive under the Steam user's home and the panel names that path beside the manual route through Decky's developer mode. What the last update did is said once rather than kept: the next check that answers lets go of an outcome nobody can act on, and the one that stays is the failed install that kept a release, which goes when the file does - installed by hand, deleted, or superseded because this device is already on that version - and a successful update removes that file itself. Installing restarts Steam's interface, which is said before the press, along with the fact that only the download can be stopped. What that window is told afterwards is bounded rather than open-ended: the backend it is asking is the one being replaced, so when it stops answering for longer than a restart takes, the window says the update was handed over and offers a way out, and the outcome is read from the durable record by the panel that comes back. The same is true on the backend's side of that boundary: an installer that exits without reporting settles the operation it was started for, so a device whose install never reached Decky can be told what happened and can try again, rather than holding one update open until something reloads the plugin. Automatic checking is armed by table-search activity and paced, one request at a time, and switching it off stops both the checking and the offer; **Check now** is the press that ignores the arming and joins a check that is already running rather than describing it. What a screen is told leads with the newest thing this device knows: a finding older than a check that failed is named as something found then, the panel withholds its press until a check answers again, and Advanced still carries both the finding and the reason the last attempt did not finish. Reading what a deletion would refuse changes nothing either, which is what the screen saying nothing is deleted by looking means and why the panel reader is allowed to press it: that report asks the updater what is happening and is answered from this process and the durable record, without settling anything. Reading the plugin's status changes nothing about an update: folding in what a detached installer left, writing down when a start time in this clock's future was first seen, and removing a recovery archive this plugin has outgrown all happen where the device is allowed to change - loading, polling an update, starting one, refusing a deletion, and the background tick - because the panel polls that status and so do read-only helpers whose whole value is that looking does not change what they are looking at. An update in flight holds down everything a plugin replacement would interrupt, and it is the panel that adopts it - the window that started it dies with the panel the moment any modal opens, so the press leads back into that window rather than starting a second update.

Decky can invoke uninstall semantics during update and reinstall, so `_uninstall()` preserves settings, profiles, and managed Cheat Engine and table data: it runs on an ordinary plugin update, and deleting the managed root there would destroy the user's own tables, authorizations and downloaded Cheat Engine every time the plugin updates. Removal is an explicit user action instead, and there are two of them. **Manage** removes one exact stored table under the per-table boundary described above. **Advanced → Prepare for removal** handles the fixed bulk scopes and refuses them while anything is still executing out of that tree: a Cheat Engine process CE Decky owns, a managed installation still unpacking into it, or a table download that still owns a staged file. Neither restores Steam state, because CE Decky never writes any: it reads AppDetails, install folders and shortcut storage for identity and owns nothing there to give back.

After bulk deletion, frontend managed authority and in-flight read generations are invalidated immediately. Status and advisory records are reconciled before the workflow settles, including after an uncertain reply; a refresh failure is logged separately and never reverses a committed deletion. A refusal is the case that is not uncertain: the backend checks before it touches anything and says so in the first words of the message, and nothing on the panel's side is reconciled for a deletion that did not happen - which is what kept it from forgetting the game the user had chosen over a Cheat Engine that was still running. The widest scope is a first run on both sides: the panel forgets its own durable choices with the files, and the updater forgets what it was holding in memory because that file could not be written, since storage that will not take writes is exactly why somebody reaches for it.

The bridge automatically attempts to return foreground ownership to the verified game's visible window after attach, dialog suppression and cheat interaction. Attempts are bounded and stop when foreground ownership is already correct. Missing capability, multiple eligible windows and refused activation are diagnostic outcomes. A successful Win32 foreground readback is not a claim that Gamescope controller input recovered; that remains an on-device check.

A new Manage confirmation uses the displayed holder identities after refresh. A newly appeared holder requires another confirmation; games that moved to another table are skipped. Revoke never stops a replacement session. Compatibility survives profile-state repair as history without a current match, and changing target executables requires new evidence even on the same Steam build. Successful autoload startup counts only after the requested leaf activation is observed complete, with no startup failure. Failure history prevents clearing Failed from reviving older success even if the positive record could not be updated.

Foreground recovery is re-armed once startup or rollback finishes, including asynchronous completion after the attach budget expired. An accepted request whose exact handle becomes foreground on a later bounded sweep is counted once as an observed confirmation; that observation still does not prove controller input or causation.

Failed writes and clears are reconciled against the exact current record when the reply is uncertain. Search and Advanced refresh their own detached lists after every clear attempt, including partial clears, without repeating a committed mutation. An unreadable readback is described as an unknown outcome. Invalid failure epochs are visible through the existing repair reason and Clear all rewrites an empty corrupt record too. A stopped selected game still compares its readable Steam build ID; other inactive historical games remain unknown. Device-wide Manage without a selected game shows one neutral historical success per exact table, choosing the newest observation and then the lowest AppID for ties, without claiming a current-build match.

After a confirmed manual activation, Search and Manage receive the new compatibility history even when the separate remembered-cheat or automatic-loading preference write fails. That persistence failure remains visible. Case-only differences in a Windows process basename do not change compatibility identity.

```

`docs/DEVELOPMENT.md`:

```md
# Development, validation, and releases

## Toolchain and repository layout

Portable, token-efficient validation is a project priority. `scripts/qa.py` is the standard-library-only control plane and the default entrypoint on Windows, Linux, CI, and the Steam Machine. A Python-only checkout can perform repository and backend-focused work; Node is a lazy frontend/build dependency, not a universal development prerequisite.

- Python 3.11 or newer
- Node.js 18 or newer
- pnpm 9.15.9, pinned by `package.json`

The Python backend has no runtime package-install step on SteamOS. Pure-Python runtime dependencies are pinned with hashes in `requirements-runtime.lock` and committed as `py_modules/vendor`, because the official Decky Store builder copies `py_modules/` as the repository holds it and installs nothing; both packagers ship that tree. **The committed runtime dependency tree** below is how it is rebuilt and what checks it. `requirements-dev.txt` repeats those exact pins for local tests and adds test tooling. Frontend packages are build dependencies and are not shipped as `node_modules`.

The root is intentionally the repository control plane, not a document folder. Keep these files at the root:

- `main.py`, `plugin.json`, `package.json`, `src/`, `dist/`, and `py_modules/` follow Decky Loader and its build conventions;
- `py_modules/stdlib_fallback/` contains verbatim CPython 3.11.7 `xml`, `html`,
  and `_markupbase` compatibility assets for Decky's stripped PyInstaller
  runtime; keep their pinned source, license, package smoke, and
  import-on-missing behavior synchronized;
- `py_modules/stdlib_fallback/python314/pathlib_types.py` is verbatim CPython
  3.14.8 `Lib/pathlib/types.py`. `ce_decky/runtime_compat.py` loads only this
  missing submodule on Python 3.14 before anyio/httpcore import; a native module
  and parent package stay authoritative. Its full license ships from defaults;
- `rollup.config.js`, `tsconfig*.json`, `pytest.ini`, and `requirements-dev.txt` use normal tool discovery and short commands;
- `.editorconfig`, `.gitattributes`, and `.gitignore` must cover the entire tree and keep Windows-to-SteamOS text handling predictable;
- `README.md`, `AGENTS.md`, `CHANGELOG.md`, and `LICENSE` must be easy to discover and are also release/legal entry points;
- `defaults/THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` and `defaults/licenses/` are the same kind of entry point and sit there for one reason: the Decky CLI packages a fixed set of top-level files and strips the `defaults/` prefix from everything under it, so this is the only path by which a notice reaches the Store artifact. Both packagers put them at the root of the archive.

Moving these into a generic `config/` or `docs/` directory would require non-standard flags, complicate upstream Decky reuse, and save no agent context. Generated files belong under ignored `build/` or `artifacts/`.

## Dependency restore

Let the selected validation profile restore only what it needs:

```powershell
python scripts/qa.py --bootstrap
```

Exact pinned packages already present in the active Python are reused; otherwise the Python environment is cached in `.venv` by the SHA-256 of `requirements-dev.txt`. When frontend work is selected, bootstrap invokes exact `pnpm@9.15.9` through Corepack and records the `package.json`/lock fingerprint in `node_modules`; unchanged environments are not restored again. The ordinary runner calls `node`, TypeScript, Vitest, and Rollup directly and never asks whatever globally installed `pnpm` happens to be active to inspect or mutate the checkout.

Use read-only discovery when diagnosing a fresh machine:

```powershell
python scripts/qa.py --check-env
```

Do not update `pnpm-lock.yaml` incidentally. A dependency change must update the manifest and lockfile together, explain why the pin changed, and run the full gate.

### Local frontend fallback

The resident Cheat Engine bridge is Lua, so it is validated by running the exact shipped script under a stock interpreter against a Cheat Engine API stub: the production Python renderers produce the descriptor and control files, the real bridge consumes them, and the production Python parser validates the status it writes. Any `lua`, `lua5.4`, `lua5.3` or `luajit` on `PATH` is discovered lazily and reported by `--check-env`; without one the stage skips locally and remains authoritative in CI, which installs `lua5.4`. Never install an interpreter on a SteamOS target to make it run.

When frontend source must be changed from an environment that cannot restore the pinned Node dependency tree, use the development-only fallback instead of hand-editing `dist/index.js` or introducing a second production bundler:

```powershell
python scripts/frontend_fallback.py
```

The fallback requires any TypeScript 5.x `tsc` on `PATH`, uses `tsconfig.sandbox.json` plus the repository shims, validates relative project imports, and emits inspectable ES modules only under ignored `build/frontend-fallback/`. It does not write `dist/index.js`, does not run Decky's Rollup preset, and does not qualify a plugin package. Its purpose is to let constrained environments make and statically validate normal `src/` changes while keeping the authoritative build path unchanged.

The official build remains `pnpm run build` / `rollup -c`. `rollup.config.js` stamps each successful official bundle with a digest of the frontend sources and build-control files. `scripts/package_plugin.py` requires that digest to match before packaging and excludes the stamp itself from the release ZIP. Therefore a development branch may temporarily carry a stale bootstrap `dist/index.js`, but stale output cannot be packaged accidentally. CI and release always run the pinned Rollup build before bundle smoke and packaging.

## Validation profiles

Use the smallest profile that covers the change. One profile is documented elsewhere because it belongs with what it builds: `--profile store` is under **The artifact the Store builds**.

### Automatic iteration profile

This is the default command after a change:

```powershell
python scripts/qa.py
```

It uses working-tree paths, or the files in `HEAD` when the tree is clean, to select direct pytest dependents, frontend component/core checks, bundling, packaging, and repository guards. Full stdout/stderr and timings are stored under `build/qa/<run-id>/`; the terminal receives only a bounded summary. A non-clean run also writes `qa-failures.json` with the exact failing command and a short tail.

### Focused profile

During implementation, run the narrowest relevant selection. Both halves have one, and they combine into a single run:

```powershell
python scripts/qa.py --pytest tests/test_profiles.py
python scripts/qa.py --pytest tests/test_network_prod.py::test_partial_stream_failure_removes_download_staging
python scripts/qa.py --vitest tests/uiModel.test.ts
python scripts/qa.py --pytest tests/test_profiles.py --vitest tests/providerCatalog.test.tsx
python scripts/qa.py --vitest tests/workflowUi.test.tsx --name "holds off the flags"
python scripts/qa.py --pytest tests/test_service.py --name "quiesce"
```

`pytest.ini` supplies the production Python path, so commands are the same on PowerShell and POSIX shells.

`qa.py` is the routed entrypoint and stays the one to use. A few things need pytest directly, and mutation checking is the usual one: break the guard you just wrote, confirm the test that names it fails, restore. That run needs the interpreter `qa.py` itself selects, because the system Python has no pytest:

```bash
./.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests/test_session_protocol.py -q
```

Run it from the repository root. `pytest.ini` puts both the root and `py_modules` on the path, so a test importing release tooling from `scripts` resolves the same way a test importing `ce_decky` does.

`--name` narrows either selection to the cases whose name matches, through each runner's own filter - `-k` for pytest, `-t` for vitest - because one case of the component suite is under two seconds against the file's forty-five. It needs a `--pytest` or a `--vitest` beside it: on its own it would narrow nothing and leave a run that looks focused and is the whole gate. A name that matches nothing fails the stage and says so, because both runners report it as a success otherwise: `vitest` skips every test in the file and exits green, and `pytest` collects nothing, prints not one character and exits 5. The two runners read the expression differently - `-k` is an expression and `-t` is text - so a phrase is joined into the expression that means the same thing, and one somebody wrote with `and`, `or` or brackets is passed through as theirs. `--name` repeats: the cases matching any of them run, so one run reaches a case in each of two files, and the stage fails only when none of them matched anything, so the case count it prints is what says whether each one did. `--vitest` takes a path or a vitest filename pattern and runs the component stage against that alone, which is seconds against the half a minute the whole stage costs. It type-checks nothing, because vitest compiles through esbuild: `--profile frontend` remains the gate for a frontend change, exactly as the backend profile is after a focused `--pytest`. A pattern that matches no file fails the stage rather than passing empty.

A component query that finds nothing prints the page as rows rather than markup: every element with a `data-testid` and the words in it, then the page's visible text, stylesheet and scripts left out and the whole bounded (`tests/setup/compactDomErrors.ts`). Testing Library's own dump is the container's markup cut at a few thousand characters, and on this panel the cut lands inside the first card, so the rows a failure is about were never printed.

`dist/index.js` is built rather than written, and a failed frontend build removes it. The next run's first stage is the repository check, which then reports it as a missing required file: read that as the build having failed, rebuild with `--profile frontend --stage frontend-build`, and read the failure that stage prints rather than the one the repository check printed. The check names this itself when the bundle is the file that is missing.

Where only the types are in question between two edits, `--stage` runs that one stage of the profile and nothing else, which is under two seconds:

```bash
python scripts/qa.py --profile frontend --stage frontend-typecheck
```

### Proving a regression against an earlier revision

A regression that passes on the commit it was written against says nothing about the defect it was written for, so a review round ends by running the new tests with the production source rolled back to the reviewed head and expecting them to fail. `scripts/qa_baseline_check.py` is that check:

```bash
python3 scripts/qa_baseline_check.py --rev <reviewed-head> --vitest tests/providerCatalog.test.tsx
python3 scripts/qa_baseline_check.py --rev <reviewed-head> --pytest tests/test_github_discovery_prod.py
python3 scripts/qa_baseline_check.py --rev <reviewed-head> --vitest tests/workflowUi.test.tsx --name "the new case" --name "the other new case"
```

`--name` narrows the selection exactly as `qa.py --name` does, which is what makes a file of a thousand cases affordable to prove a regression in. The revision's own `qa.py` runs the selection, so one too old to take `--name` is refused by name with exit 2 rather than read as a run that failed.

It creates a temporary `git worktree` at that revision, puts this checkout's `tests/` on top of it so the tests being proved are the new ones, shares the restored dependency trees rather than restoring them again, runs the same routed selection there, and prints the tests that failed. The checkout being worked in is never written to, which is what makes it safe in a workflow whose every round ends in a commit, a push and an install onto a device. It exits non-zero when the selection passes at that revision, because a regression that passes there proves nothing, and again when the run fails without naming a test, because a run that could not start is not a proved defect. `--expect-pass` inverts it for a control case: a test asserting behaviour that is deliberately unchanged should still pass at the baseline.

It answers for one half only. That the selection passes on the current tree is what the ordinary routed run already said, and this never repeats it.

### Full gate

This is the ordinary CI and pre-handoff gate, and the only full one:

```powershell
python scripts/qa.py --profile release
```

Run it in the foreground, one at a time, and wait for it: `build/qa/reuse.json` is a single file with no lock, so two concurrent runs overwrite each other's record of what passed, and the component suite's `waitFor` budgets are written for a machine that is not simultaneously running a gate.

Run this once after focused iteration. It runs the complete Python suite, strict TypeScript, component/core checks, the official Rollup build, built-bundle smoke, the plugin package and its probe, and repository guards. There is no second, package-less full profile: the packaging costs half a second and every production change here ends in an install that wants it, so a choice between the two was only ever a chance to run both.

`--stage` runs only the stages it names, and it may be repeated: `--stage frontend-build --stage frontend-component` runs both, in the order the profile schedules them. A name the profile does not schedule is refused and the message lists what it does schedule. A run that packages also prints the exact `target_plugin_install.py` command for the artifact and digest it just produced, on any host that can install one.

A stage whose inputs have not moved since it passed is reused rather than run again, printed as `REUSED`. The fingerprint is every tracked file's path and contents, plus the stage's own command and interpreter and the two restored dependency trees' own markers, so any edit anywhere invalidates every stage. Contents rather than timestamps because the gate rewrites `dist/index.js` on every frontend build, with identical bytes, and a timestamp would have it invalidating its own reuse each time it ran. Packaging is never reused, because its work is the artifact rather than its verdict, and neither are the `live` and `direct` provider profiles, which exist to observe somebody else's server as it is now and are the one thing an unchanged tree says nothing about. An explicitly named test or stage always runs too, because naming one is an instruction to run it. `--no-reuse` runs everything regardless.

Two things bound what reuse can cost. The record lives under ignored `build/`, so a fresh checkout has none and the authoritative CI run always executes every stage. And the one stage whose output later stages depend on is the frontend build: a source change moves the fingerprint, so nothing is reused and the build runs, and if it were skipped anyway `package_plugin.py` refuses a `dist/index.js` that is stale for the current sources. That check is about the bundle matching its sources, not about the bundle being untampered: editing the built file directly still packages, exactly as it did before any of this. The official Rollup build is authoritative for `dist/index.js`; constrained development environments may commit normal frontend source/tests after the local fallback, but packaging is blocked until the pinned build has refreshed the source digest.

Because `dist/index.js` is tracked and every profile that builds the frontend rewrites it, run `frontend` or `release` before committing frontend source, and stage the rebuilt bundle in the same commit. A commit of the source alone is followed by the next build rewriting a file that commit already claimed to be finished with, which costs a second commit, a second release run and a second install, and leaves the package that was just verified belonging to no commit.

The complete Python suite uses POSIX executable fixtures, symlink semantics, and POSIX-to-Wine `Z:` conversion. On Windows the runner searches installed WSL distributions and uses one only when Python 3.11+ and the pinned dev dependencies are already valid. Otherwise the backend-full stage is `INCOMPLETE`; it does not run the known-incompatible native suite or attempt privileged OS provisioning. Linux/CI remains authoritative. Never add broad skips to make security/path tests appear portable.

### Reading a screen instead of photographing it

A screenshot is the honest record of a frame and a poor way to answer how many rows fit, whether a button is disabled, or what a footer says. This reads the same screen as text:

```bash
python3 scripts/target_panel_read.py --open --metrics
python3 scripts/target_panel_read.py --testid manage-footer
python3 scripts/target_panel_read.py --json
python3 scripts/target_panel_read.py --reopen --press 'Advanced…' --metrics
python3 scripts/target_panel_read.py --press 'imported-table-33a60e6b:Use'   # reported, and it writes
python3 scripts/target_panel_read.py --press 'cheat-row-1337099264:active'   # a switch, by the name of the control
python3 scripts/target_panel_read.py --choose '<game name> · non-Steam'      # one option of a dropdown, through Steam's menu
python3 scripts/target_panel_read.py --describe review-findings             # one row's whole text and every control in it
python3 scripts/target_panel_read.py --press table-code-footer:Back          # navigation beside a modal's dense block
python3 scripts/target_panel_read.py --wait-for 'runtime-row:Connected' --wait-seconds 60
python3 scripts/target_panel_read.py --find cheat-row-61 --describe cheat-row-61   # pages to that row, naming every turn
python3 scripts/target_panel_read.py --find-text 'its script has not run yet'      # pages until some row says it, and names that row
```

The count a screen leads with is a row of its own, so it reads as text rather than from a capture: `cheats-summary` is the header of Configure cheats (`1 active (1 script)`, and what the table holds), and `pinned-status` is the panel's line about pinned cheats it cannot draw.

It serialises every surface this plugin is drawing: each row by its `data-testid`, the text actually rendered, the controls beside it with their disabled and focused state, how many of its lines are clipped, whether the panel is drawing its mascot at all, and with `--metrics` the height of each row and of the surface. Buttons that sit in no row, such as Steam's full-width **Load table & start CE** and **Configure cheats**, which carry no test id, are listed under an `untagged-controls` row of the surface they are on, which `--wait-for` and a scoped `--press untagged-controls:<name>` take like any other row. That is a dozen lines where a capture is a megabyte, and it answers the questions a layout change is about. `target_screenshot.py` stays for what a picture is actually for: colour, overlap, and anything about the frame itself.

`--open` opens the quick access panel on this plugin's own page first, through Steam's own `MenuStore.OpenQuickAccessMenu` reached the way `@decky/ui` reaches it, and Decky's own `deckyState.setActivePlugin`. `--reopen` closes it through Steam's own `CloseSideMenus` and opens it again, and it is the one to use after changing anything the backend holds: the panel re-reads the backend when it comes back into view, so a panel that never went away has no reason to have noticed, and reading it then reports the state before the change as though it were the state after it. Both are API calls rather than injected input. Past that first screen, `--press <name>` activates one of this plugin's own controls by the name on it and can be repeated to go deeper, which is how a modal is reached without anybody at the device. **Any of this plugin's controls, and every press is reported.** This is a testing tool, and the screen behind a press that writes is still a screen somebody has to look at, so **Use**, **Apply** and **Delete** are reachable; what that costs is a rule rather than a refusal. Each press is named on its own line as it lands, with the surface it was found on, a run that pressed anything ends with the list of what it pressed in order, and `--json` carries the same list. Repeat that list when reporting what the run found: a press the operator was never told about is the defect the rule exists to prevent, not the press itself. Say it before driving a device that is not yours to write to, and prefer a read to a press where a read answers the question. Two limits remain, and neither is about which name is allowed. A name that is on more than one control presses nothing and reports where each of them is, because **Search** opens the search screen from the panel and spends a provider request inside it, **Cancel** leaves a dialog and stops a running Cheat Engine installation on the panel, and **Use** is on every row of a list; write `<data-testid>:<name>` to name the one row instead, which is how `--press table-row:Search` reaches the search screen and `--press imported-table-33a60e6b:Use` reaches one row's own press. And a disabled control is reported as disabled rather than activated. A running game and Steam's own interface are what still needs the maintainer.

Five more things a device session needs, each of which was a dead end before it existed. A switch is pressed by the name of the control rather than by a label, because Steam draws one as a `div` with no name at all: this plugin marks its own with `data-switch`, the reader reports each one with what it is showing, and `--press <row>:<name>` flips it - without that, a reader could report every row of a screen and reach none of the switches, which is most of what this product is. `--choose <option>` picks one option of a dropdown by the text a reader sees, which is Steam's own context menu rather than anything this plugin drew, so it opens the control, waits for the menu, matches the option, and where it cannot, closes the menu again and prints the options that were there; it is a write and is reported exactly as a press is. `--describe <data-testid>` prints one row's whole text, up to four thousand characters, and every control inside it with its tag, role, classes and `data-` marks, which is both how a finding block several sentences long is read in full and how a control this reader cannot yet name is identified. And `--wait-for <data-testid>:<text>` waits, bounded by `--wait-seconds`, until that row says that: a stop, an install or an activation is a screen that is still doing something, and polling it by hand is how a walk turns into a busy loop. `--find <data-testid>` turns the pages of the screen in front, **Next ›** until the row is on it or Next is disabled and then **‹ Previous** back to the first page, at most forty turns each way; every turn is a press and is named like one, and a screen with no pager presses nothing and says so. A press returns once the click is dispatched, not once what it asked the backend for has happened: **Clear** was reported pressed seconds before the backend cleared the hold, so a probe read straight afterwards still showed it. Read the outcome through `--wait-for`, or after the backend log says it happened.

### What Steam's own JavaScript says the library holds

The panel's game list comes from `SteamClient.InstallFolder.GetInstallFolders` and from `appStore.allApps`, and what those return on a device is not answerable from memory:

```bash
python3 scripts/target_steam_library_probe.py install-folders
python3 scripts/target_steam_library_probe.py library-apps --json
python3 scripts/target_steam_library_probe.py app-details --app-id 220
```

It asks one of those named questions, read only, through Steam's own CEF endpoint in the `SharedJSContext` page, reusing the DevTools client `target_ui_freeze_probe.py` already carries. It evaluates no JavaScript from the caller, injects no input, and prints every field of each record rather than the ones this plugin happens to use, because the field that settles a question is usually one nobody had typed yet. It runs on the device, like every other target helper.

What it is for is comparing Steam's answer with the device's own files: `steamapps/appmanifest_*.acf` is what an install is, and `userdata/*/config/shortcuts.vdf` is what a local non-Steam shortcut is. A disagreement between the two is the finding. One run of this established that a Steam Deck's library offered 39 non-Steam shortcuts while the device's own store held 6, which is Steam syncing a library rather than installs.

### What the gate's suites spend their time on

`qa.py` says what each stage cost and nothing about why. This says which tests those seconds are in:

```powershell
python3 scripts/qa_durations.py --top 25
python3 scripts/qa_durations.py --frontend
python3 scripts/qa_durations.py --json
```

It runs the same suites the gate runs, through the interpreter and Node `qa.py` itself resolves, and adds only a reporting flag: `--durations` for pytest and vitest's own per-file timings for the component suite. It reports the total, the sum of the rows it printed, and each row. `--timeout` bounds it and defaults to fifteen minutes.

Use it before optimising anything about the gate, because the answer is routinely a handful of tests rather than the suite: one run of it found 91 seconds of a 108 second stage in 30 tests out of 906, and the worst of them was a fixture re-summing its own list on every append rather than anything the product does. Two kinds of finding come out of it and they are not the same. A test that is slow by accident is fixed in the test, and the fixture must be proved identical afterwards rather than assumed to be. A test that is slow because it waits on a production interval is fixed by naming that interval and letting the test set its own, and only where the test is about what the code decides rather than about the pacing itself; a test that is about the pacing keeps it.

A measurement taken with this helper is reproducible and worth recording. One taken by hand, with a stopwatch or a pasted `pytest` line, is not.

### Live provider profile

Live catalog checks are explicit, read-only toward providers, and excluded from ordinary CI. They use the production transport, parsers, acquisition manager, archive inspection, and content-addressed `TableStore`; downloaded files and imported tables exist only below pytest's temporary directory and are never executed.

```powershell
python scripts/qa.py --profile live
```

The fixed cases cover known FearLess attachments, GitHub release assets from an exact repository source, one GitHub repository found by searching the index whose table is committed in its tree, direct Playground files, one current The Cheat Script Yandex artifact, and one VGTimes table through the site's own countdown and challenge chain, which is slow by design. The Playground countdowns run concurrently and each provider follows the full production acquisition/import path. Because provider content and challenge policy are mutable external state, record failures as compatibility evidence and keep deterministic local-server/fixture tests authoritative in CI.

### Direct provider acceptance profile

Use this gate while developing the primary no-interaction catalog workflow:

```powershell
python scripts/qa.py --profile direct
```

It runs only known public artifacts marked `direct_provider`, through production transport, parsing, acquisition, archive inspection, SHA verification, import, and temporary storage. Browser handoff or file-picker fallback is a test failure. Terminal output is one bounded stage summary; full mutable-provider output remains under `build/qa/`. The profile is opt-in, excluded from CI, and never replaces the deterministic tests. A red provider is compatibility evidence to investigate.

### Release profile

Before creating a tag:

```powershell
python scripts/qa.py --profile release
```

`release` is the only full gate, and it creates and verifies the deterministic plugin archive as part of itself. It installs nothing while doing so: the runtime dependencies are the committed `py_modules/vendor`, and packaging refuses a tree that does not match its recorded digest rather than rebuilding one. The tag workflow repeats this profile on Ubuntu; a local pass is preparation, not a substitute for GitHub Actions or on-target validation on SteamOS.

### Authoritative CI results

GitHub Actions is the authoritative complete Linux backend gate for pushed production, build, dependency, test, packaging, and release changes. Inspect it without leaving the terminal:

```bash
gh run list --workflow ci.yml --branch <branch> --limit 1 --json headSha,status,conclusion,databaseId
gh run view <run-id> --log-failed
```

On SteamOS `gh`, like Node, is installed into `~/.local/bin`, which a
non-login shell does not have on PATH: prefix these with
`PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"`. `qa.py` adds that directory to its own PATH,
and `qa.py --check-env` names where it found `node` and `gh`.

The first is what proves a green run belongs to the exact head, which is the
only thing `AGENTS.md` treats as ready: a plain `gh run list` prints no commit,
so it cannot answer that. On a pull request the required run is the
`pull_request` one on the PR branch rather than anything on `main`. Read it when
the maintainer asks whether CI is green, and after pushing a fix for a run that
was red; a push otherwise ends the work without waiting. When they have asked
for the wait, one command does it rather than a series of them:

```bash
until gh run list --workflow ci.yml --branch <branch> --limit 5 --json headSha,status,conclusion \
  -q '.[] | select(.headSha == "<exact-head>" and .status == "completed") | .conclusion' \
  | grep .; do sleep 20; done
```

It ends by printing `success` or `failure`, which is the answer being waited
for; `grep` without `-q` is what puts it on the screen. Five rows rather than
one because a run started after this one, for a head that is not this one,
would otherwise hide it forever.

The runner prints the names of the cases that failed in every stage that failed, read with the terminal's colour codes taken out because `vitest` colours those lines on the CI runner, and, for the first stage that failed and for the first stage that could not run, the runner's own account of the first of them - the assertion, its diff and the file and line it is on - each headed by its stage key and followed by its rerun command. It reads from each runner's own banner rather than from the end of the log: `pytest` finishes with a summary a tail reaches, `vitest` finishes with a count and a footer while the assertion is hundreds of lines earlier, and reading a frontend failure used to mean running the same selection a second time with a filter on the output. A stage that is not a test run, or one that died before it could report, keeps its tail, because there the last thing said is the whole of what happened. Both are needed here: a stage that could not run is what a collection error looks like, its cause is nowhere else in a CI log, and the run directory holding `qa-failures.json` is thrown away with the runner. Reproduce the exact selection through `scripts/qa.py` before editing; do not replace a red required gate with a narrower one. If `gh` is unavailable, use the repository's existing Git credential for read-only GitHub REST calls and never print the token. Documentation-only changes need repository QA, not a CI wait.

## Decky runtime compatibility and upstream watch

`scripts/decky_compat_probe.py` takes an exact plugin ZIP and official Linux
x86-64 Decky executable. It verifies the executable SHA-256, validates the ZIP
through the existing package probe, unpacks it into temporary storage, and
executes `scripts/decky_compat_payload.py` in that runtime. The child exercises
the packaged import graph, real asynchronous HTTP and streaming download with
a local fixture, parsers, compression, offline tables and real access-denial
state refusals. It also starts an innocuous system child through the production
clean environment and proves a cancelled worker is drained on a healthy loop;
that does not exercise Decky's real unload sequence. It creates no plugin
instance, launches no Cheat Engine and reads no user state. Expected structured
results and the process exit must agree.

```bash
python scripts/decky_compat_probe.py --plugin <exact-plugin.zip> --decky <exact-PluginLoader> --sha256 <runtime-sha256> --version <Decky-tag> --output build/decky-compatibility.json
```

Only the reviewed digest in `scripts/decky_compat_pin.json` may run locally.
Unknown candidate executables require disposable GitHub CI; the PyInstaller
resource-tracker diversion is a diagnostic route, not a Decky API. The child has
a temporary home, a clean environment, bounded execution/output and an owned
process group. `--python` is an ordinary Python control and supplies no frozen
Decky evidence. PASS covers the named backend/artifact checks, not real QAM
rendering, controller navigation, Decky lifecycle or every Proton workflow.
`tests/test_decky_compat_probe.py` runs the real packaged pair and a deliberately
broken variant when `CE_DECKY_COMPAT_PLUGIN_DIR` and `CE_DECKY_COMPAT_RUNTIME`
are supplied; `CE_DECKY_REQUIRE_FROZEN=1` refuses missing inputs. Ordinary
validation remains `python scripts/qa.py`, including these tests.

CI retains the Python 3.11 release and Store gates and shares the already-built
package with a focused Python 3.14 job and the pinned actual Decky runtime.
The same job checks the prior v3.2.8 frozen runtime as a compatibility baseline;
fetch it with `scripts/decky_compat_monitor.py fetch-pin --baseline --output
<previous-PluginLoader>`. Its exact digest is also pinned, and its diagnostic
entry route is exercised only in disposable CI. Set
`CE_DECKY_COMPAT_BASELINE_RUNTIME` to that path for the baseline test.
No second frontend/package build is introduced. The new `decky-runtime` job
must pass before publication. Required CI never moves its supported pin based
on a new upstream release.

`.github/workflows/decky-compatibility.yml` answers a different question from
required CI: whether the latest published CE Decky release, however old, still
works in the Decky its users are moving to. It is tied to no CE Decky tag and
runs on a daily timer. `scripts/decky_compat_monitor.py` coordinates it with
standard-library-only GitHub REST calls.

The unit is a pair of exact artifacts: one Decky runtime (tag and `PluginLoader`
SHA-256) and one CE Decky release (version and ZIP SHA-256). The current pairs
are the latest published CE Decky release against Decky's latest stable release
and its newest prerelease, when that prerelease is newer. A new Decky release, a
replaced Decky executable under an existing tag and a new CE Decky release each
make a new pair, and each pair is tested once. A day with no new pair costs a
few API reads. A Decky release whose executable is not attached yet is a pair
that waits. The pair key carries a channel, `github`, because GitHub Releases
are the only place CE Decky is published; it is not listed in the Decky Store.

`discover` reads everything first and writes the ledger only after: the latest
CE Decky release, its `SHA256SUMS`, the archive itself checked by
`gh attestation verify` against this repository's `release.yml`, and Decky's
release feed. A failed read leaves the ledger as it was, and fails the run, so
an outage of GitHub's own API is one mail a day while it lasts; only a pair's
downloads are retried silently, below. Each untested pair
becomes one `probe` job, named `probe (Decky <tag> × CE Decky <version>)`, so
the failure mail names what broke. That job has read-only permission and no
token, because it runs unreviewed Decky executables. It checks out the CE Decky
release's own tag and runs the probe from that tag: the probe reaches into the
plugin's internals, and only the copy written with a release knows that
release, so a newer probe never produces a false failure for an older release.
That makes the probe's arguments and result fields a contract with every
published release; `tests/test_decky_compat_probe.py` holds them. Beside the
candidate run, the same probe runs in the Decky that release pinned in its own
`scripts/decky_compat_pin.json`, which is the control:

| Control (pinned Decky) | Candidate | Recorded as |
|---|---|---|
| PASS | PASS | `COMPATIBLE` |
| PASS | FAIL | `BROKEN`: this Decky breaks this release |
| PASS | INCOMPLETE | `UNVERIFIABLE`: the probe cannot run in this Decky |
| anything else | anything | `PROBE_BROKEN`: the probe or runner broke, not the plugin |
| none, the candidate is the pin | PASS / other | `COMPATIBLE` / `PROBE_BROKEN` |

A release whose tag has no probe, 0.9.29 and older, is `UNSUPPORTED`. A pair
whose inputs could not be downloaded is not judged: it stays untested and the
next run asks again. `STATUS.md` on the ledger branch lists the current pairs,
their result, when and by which run, and each pair's key. That page is the
current answer; a failure mail is only the moment something changed.

A run fails, and GitHub sends its failed-workflow mail, when a new pair is
anything but `COMPATIBLE`, and when a current pair has waited three days
without a result, which is then repeated at most every three days. A problem
already recorded stays silent on later runs and stays on `STATUS.md`. Running
the workflow by hand with `retest` set to a key from `STATUS.md`, or to
`current`, tests those pairs again; nothing else repeats one, and a repeat
keeps the earlier answers in that pair's history. No issues, SMTP credentials
or mail service are involved. The monitor never moves the pin required CI uses:
a `COMPATIBLE` new Decky says the pin can be moved, by a reviewed change.

State lives in this repository, on the dedicated `compatibility-monitor-state`
branch, because nothing else GitHub offers a workflow outlives it: artifacts
expire and caches are evicted. The branch shares no history with `main` and
holds three files: `decky-compatibility.json`, the ledger the workflow reads;
`STATUS.md`; and a `README.md` saying what the branch is. It is never merged,
rebased or turned into a pull request. Every write is one commit holding the
ledger and the page together, made only when either changed, so the page
always describes the ledger it was committed with. Each commit says what
changed, `Track Decky v3.4.0 × CE Decky 0.9.30` or `Record BROKEN for ...`, so
the branch's history is the monitor's log. The ref only fast-forwards from the
commit the run read, so a writer holding an older ledger is refused rather
than writing over a newer one.

Missing or unreadable state fails visibly; never reset it to empty. The ledger
refuses writes at 512 KiB rather than discarding history. `discover` and
`record` alone receive contents-write, and because that permission is not
branch-scoped, the coordinator refuses every write but a tree of the branch's
own three files, a commit with at most one parent, and a fast-forward of that
one branch, and refuses to follow a redirect with its token. `discover` also
reads attestations. Every checkout keeps no credentials.

Enable only after publishing a release that carries the probe, 0.9.30 or newer:

1. In GitHub account Settings > Notifications > System > Actions, select Email
   and Only notify for failed workflows. This account-wide choice also silences
   successful ordinary-CI mail. Ensure the intended account created, last edited
   the cron, or re-enabled the schedule; GitHub uses that actor as recipient.
2. Run this workflow manually on `main` with `initialize=true`. It creates the
   state branch as one commit with no parent, holding an empty ledger, and
   tests nothing; an existing branch is refused, never reinitialized.
3. In Settings > Rules > Rulesets, add a branch ruleset targeting
   `compatibility-monitor-state` with Restrict deletions and Block force
   pushes. The monitor only fast-forwards the branch, so neither rule gets in
   its way, and losing the branch would lose the record of what was tested.
4. Set repository variable `DECKY_COMPAT_MONITOR_ENABLED=true`. Until then,
   scheduled jobs are skipped. Set it false to stop recurring work while keeping
   the ledger. The first scheduled run tests the current pairs. A run started
   by hand always runs, switched on or not, which is how the whole chain is
   checked before the timer is trusted with it.

Coverage is what the probe covers: the packaged import graph, real asynchronous
HTTP and downloads, parsers, offline tables and state refusals in the frozen
runtime. Decky's own plugin loading, RPC and unload, the Quick Access Menu,
controller navigation and Proton are not exercised, so `COMPATIBLE` is not a
promise about them.

GitHub may delay/drop scheduled runs and disables inactive public-repository
schedules after 60 days without activity. Check the Actions page and re-enable
when necessary; ledger commits are not a proven exemption. Native notification,
schedule, Git database and attestation contracts are documented at
https://docs.github.com/en/actions/concepts/workflows-and-actions/notifications-for-workflow-runs,
https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/workflows-and-actions/events-that-trigger-workflows#schedule,
https://docs.github.com/en/rest/git/trees, https://docs.github.com/en/rest/git/commits,
https://docs.github.com/en/rest/git/refs#update-a-reference and
https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_attestation_verify.

## UI test strategy

UI confidence is split into layers so off-target automation does not pretend to emulate Steam:

1. **Pure behavior on every frontend change.** `tests/ts_core_test.cjs` tests archive member import and its password boundary, Steam identity reads against a client that exposes no launch-option setter at all, Proton classification, and fail-closed identity conflicts, without a browser.
2. **Bundle contract on every build.** `scripts/test_dist_fallback.mjs` imports `dist/index.js` with the minimum Decky/React boundary and verifies the plugin factory. Python RPC contract tests keep frontend call names synchronized with the backend.
3. **Component tests for decomposed workflows.** Vitest and Testing Library cover the extracted provider catalog component with explicit Decky API mocks: loading/results/failures, focus order, direct import, cancellation, and the imported-without-consent boundary. Prefer state/action assertions over large snapshots.
4. **Optional installed-browser harness for stable mocked screens.** On Linux/Steam Machine, `python scripts/browser_harness.py` verifies or bootstraps the exact pinned Chrome for Testing archive under ignored `build/browser-runtime/`, exports its executable only to the child QA process, and runs the browser profile; `--profile auto` combines ordinary change routing and browser QA in the same delegated run. `--check`, `--install-only`, and `--stage browser-headless-probe` cover read-only discovery, one-time bootstrap, and exact reruns without system/Flatpak installation. The pin was selected from GoogleChromeLabs `chrome-for-testing` commit `c1decc26ccd28463f6e2fe3c8d490d7a5a13adbd`, then bound to exact archive and executable size/SHA-256; the browser and archive are local QA cache and never enter plugin/source packages. Other hosts may use `CE_DECKY_BROWSER` or normal Chrome/Chromium discovery with `python scripts/qa.py --profile browser`. The probe starts one isolated process group, waits for a JavaScript-set title through loopback DevTools endpoints, records the product version, and stops the complete group before deleting its disposable profile. Build future QAM-sized screen fixtures on the same raw-CDP lifecycle before adding Playwright. Mocked screenshots are presentation regression evidence, not Decky compatibility evidence.
Three shapes of component test have failed on the CI runner and never here, and
both were the test rather than the screen. A press that starts an async action
commits its state on a microtask, so a fake clock advanced in the same statement
races it: flush the press first. And `findBy` waits for the thing it names, not
for what arrives later inside it, so awaiting a row that renders before its data
and then asserting on that data with `getBy` is the same race one level down.
Moving the focus ring is a commit of its own, after the one that rendered the
control it lands on, so awaiting that control and then reading
`document.activeElement` races it in the same way.
Wait for what the answer puts on the screen, and check an absence only after
something proves the answer arrived.

A container is not its contents, which is the same mistake one level out: a
footer whose paging depends on a fetched index is on screen before that index
arrives, so awaiting the footer and then reading an attribute the index
decides passes on a fast machine and races on a loaded one. Wrap the
assertion in `waitFor` rather than the element in `findBy`.

Keep browser tests independent of Steam private DOM/class names. Prefer stable component boundaries and accessible labels. A UI test should fail for a user-visible regression, not a harmless markup refactor.

## Packaging

Create the Decky archive with:

```powershell
python scripts/package_plugin.py
```

The deterministic ZIP is written to `artifacts/CE-Decky-v<version>.zip`. Deterministic here means reproducible from any checkout of the commit, not merely stable on one machine: timestamps are fixed and member permissions are normalized to 0644 or 0755 by the executable bit, because Git records only that one bit and a file left at 0600 in somebody's working tree would otherwise build a different archive from identical content. That is what makes the release attestation something a reader can check against their own build. It includes runtime frontend/backend files, README, licenses, and notices; it excludes source tests, Cheat Engine, tables, and the local frontend source-digest stamp. Packaging fails closed unless `dist/index.js` was produced for the current frontend sources by the official Rollup build, then imports the backend from a freshly unpacked ZIP under Python isolated mode. The release profile also runs `target_package_probe.py` against that exact artifact.

`artifacts/` and staging directories are ignored. Never commit generated archives.

### A build that is older than the release, for testing the updater

The plugin installs its own newer release, and the only way to exercise that
whole path is from a device holding a build the release is newer than. Checking
out an older commit would test the old code, and a debug override that makes
this build claim an older version would put a branch in production that exists
only for a test. So the current tree is packaged with the version strings
